docs.title: Momo documentation
docs.text:
Momo is a Go ORM that generates typed column and relation descriptors from plain Go structs, keeps SQL explicit and inspectable, builds pgvector support into the core API, and ships its own migration engine that writes reviewable SQL. It supports PostgreSQL with pgvector; capabilities states exactly what else exists and what does not. Pages are written from the code and checked in CI: every Go block compiles, and the examples run against PostgreSQL.

New here? Start with getting started.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
• Getting started: requirements, install, a first program that talks to PostgreSQL, and where the typed API starts.
  • Guide for AI coding agents: one self-contained file for an agent using Momo in an application: setup, modeling, migrations, queries, relations, vectors, errors, testing, known pitfalls and rules. Also indexed by llms.txt at the repository root.
  • Go to SQL type mapping: column type per Go type, edge values, null handling.
  • Vector search: pgvector types, metrics, limits, search settings and the binary codec.
  • MySQL and MariaDB: supported servers, DSN requirements, the capability matrix, write and locking differences, error mapping, and what is not available yet.
  • Full-text search: the tsvector column type, the match, query, rank and headline builders, and a hybrid vector plus text ranking pattern.
  • Projections: declaring a projection, From and Columns, the generated metadata, tuple rows (Row1 to Row10), the soft-delete filter.
  • Relations: declaring, loading, filtering and writing relations, with error behavior and limits.
  • Migration safety and recovery: snapshots, apply semantics, locks, failure recovery, production checklist, CLI reference.
  • Importing models from other ORMs: the GORM, Bun and Ent readers (static, they never execute your code), the momo import command, the import report and what each report kind means, and the readers that import Atlas, goose, golang-migrate and Bun migration history.
  • Coming from GORM: a call-by-call cheat sheet from GORM models, queries, relations, hooks, transactions, migrations and errors to Momo.
  • Coming from Bun: the same mapping for Bun users.
  • Coming from Ent: the same mapping for Ent users, with the momo import ent path.
  • Read replicas: WithReplicas, which statements go to a replica, reading your own writes, and what happens when a replica is down.
  • Testing applications: the momotest kit: a schema or a rolled-back transaction per test, migrations applied, fixture seeding, parallel-safe.
  • Interceptors: application-level per-handle rules that add predicates or deny typed statements, the tenant recipe, and the paths they do not cover (not a security boundary).
  • Static check for raw SQL: the momovet analyzer that reports non-constant SQL passed to the raw-SQL functions.
  • Observability hooks: the obs package: the test recorder, the N+1 relation-load detector and the momolog slog hook, and how they treat sensitive arguments.
  • Capabilities: what each database supports, what is not built, and what returns ErrUnsupported.
  • Performance: the measured hook-overhead allocation budget and the layout of the comparison benchmark suite.
  • Supported versions: Go, PostgreSQL, pgvector, PgBouncer, pgx and OS versions in CI for v0.6.0, and the stability policy.
  • Using these docs with an AI coding agent: where an agent should read, canonical patterns and a copy-paste AGENTS.md snippet.
  • API reference: every exported identifier of the core and feature packages with its doc-comment synopsis; generated by go generate.
  • Architecture: the packages that exist, how they layer and the import rules the tests enforce.
  • Upgrading: breaking changes between releases, with a rewrite recipe; pre-v1, so more can follow.
  • Contributing: prerequisites, test commands, commit messages and file headers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Runnable programs, each tested end to end in CI. See the examples index for the layout and how to add one.

  • quickstart: the root README loop: models, generate, CRUD, relations, vector search, a transaction.
  • crud-zero-null: insert, update, delete; zero value versus NULL versus default; soft delete.
  • transactions: Tx, rollback, savepoints, read-only and isolation, retry on serialization failure.
  • testing: momotest: a database or a rolled-back transaction per test, migrations applied, seeded fixtures, parallel tests.
  • relations: has-many, belongs-to, many-to-many; Load, Preload, Joined, Has, Link, CreateGraph.
  • projection-pagination: column subsets, keyset pagination with a tie-break, counting.
  • vector-search: HNSW index, nearest-neighbour queries, filters, search settings.
  • upgrade-database: change a model after production: add a column with a default, add an index, rename a column, apply with data kept, generate --check and drift.
  • custom-sql-migration: hand-written SQL migrations beside generated ones: backfill, DO $$ splitting, -- momo:no-transaction, a hand-written CONCURRENTLY index, momo.sum checksums.
  • adopt-existing-schema: put a plain-SQL database under Momo with migrate baseline (momo generate --from-db can then write the models from the database).

docs.title: Momo architecture
docs.text: This page describes the packages that exist in the repository and the rules they follow. It lists no planned packages. For what each database supports see capabilities; for exact signatures read the package documentation, which is the source of truth.

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
cmd/momo → cli         cmd/momovet (analyzer binary)
                 │
   ┌─────────────┼──────────────┐
   gen (plugin interface)       migrate ── migrate/{postgres,sqlite,mysql}
   gen/{viz,fromdb,apiquery,    │
        graphql,grpc,openapi}   │
   │                            │
   └──── schema ◄───────────────┘
            ▲
   momo (root runtime) ── dialect, vector, types
            ▲
   driver/{pgxdriver,sqlitedriver,sqlitepure,mysqldriver}

Dependency rules. Tests in internal/repocheck enforce the first rule and the two architecture rules below it; the rest are conventions that no test checks.

  1. Enforced by TestImportGraph (go list -deps): momo, dialect, schema and vector import only the standard library and each other (the root package may also import types). No driver, no golang.org/x/tools, no YAML.
  2. Enforced by TestInternalNeverImportsRoot: the internal packages the root builds on never import the root.
  3. Enforced by TestFeaturePackagesImportOnlyAllowed: the feature subpackages listed in internal/repocheck/testdata/packages.txt import only the root, the leaf packages and internal/*. TestKnownPackages forces every new package to be given a role in that file.
  4. Convention: driver/* import momo plus their database driver only.
  5. Convention: gen, migrate/*, cli and cmd/* may import golang.org/x/tools, YAML and drivers. An application binary that imports only momo and one driver never links them.
  6. Convention: generated code imports only momo, vector, types, schema and the model package.

docs.title: dialect
docs.text: dialect.Dialect describes one database: its dialect.Dialect.Name (postgres, sqlite or mysql), the MySQL dialect.Flavor (mysql or mariadb), the per-statement bind limit MaxParams and a set of capability flags such as Returning, OnConflict, OnDuplicateKey, Locking, RowValues, Savepoints, ILike and Merge. It also quotes identifiers and writes placeholders. dialect.For returns the dialect for a name and dialect.MySQLFlavor the MySQL or MariaDB variant. The query builder consults these flags and returns ErrUnsupported for what a dialect cannot do.

docs.title: schema
docs.text: The neutral description of a database schema: tables, columns, indexes, foreign keys, checks, enums, views, functions, triggers and policies. It is what the generator produces from your models, what a migration snapshot stores, and what each migration dialect inspects from a live database. schema.Load reads a stored schema and refuses a newer schema.FormatVersion with schema.ErrNewerFormat. schema.Equal and the Normalize* functions compare schemas without being fooled by spelling differences.

docs.title: momo (root runtime)
docs.text:
• Handles: DB, Tx and the Querier interface that both satisfy. momo.New(driver, opts...) builds a DB.
  • The driver contract: Driver, DriverTx and Rows, plus optional interfaces a driver can add: ErrorClassifier, Pinner (a pinned connection), Copier (bulk copy), Batcher (several statements in one round trip) and PoolStater.
  • Typed statements: Select, Insert, Update, Delete, SoftDelete and Merge, built from generated column descriptors (Column[T], NullColumn[T], VectorColumn[V]) and expression builders. Query values are immutable: each method returns a modified copy.
  • Raw SQL escape hatches: momo.Exec, momo.Scalars, momo.Query, momo.QueryRows, momo.SQL, momo.TypedSQL and RawSubquery, with ? positional and @name named placeholders.
  • Relations: generated Relation descriptors, Load, LoadAll, Preload and the join and write helpers; see relations.
  • Transactions, savepoints and pinned connections (DB.OnConn).
  • Handle options: hooks (WithHook), interceptors (WithInterceptor, see interceptors), read replicas (WithReplicas, see replicas), limits (WithMaxParams, WithMaxInList) and a clock for tests.
  • Errors: one Error type and the Err* sentinels. Match them with errors.Is, never on message text.

docs.title: vector
docs.text: The pgvector value types vector.Vector, vector.HalfVector, vector.SparseVector and vector.Bits, each a sql.Scanner and driver.Valuer with a Validate method, and ErrInvalidVector. A vector field declares its dimension with the tag dim:<n>; the Go type selects the SQL type. See vectors.

docs.title: types
docs.text: Codec types for columns that have no plain Go equivalent: types.JSON[T], types.Date, types.TimeOfDay, types.UUID, types.Hstore and the full-text types.TSVector and types.TSQuery. See type mapping.

docs.title: driver/*
docs.text: Package Database Notes driver/pgxdriver PostgreSQL pgx v5 pool or database/sql; copy and batch driver/sqlitedriver SQLite cgo, not on Windows; vectors through sqlite-vec driver/sqlitepure SQLite pure Go, no vectors driver/mysqldriver MySQL 8.4, 9.7 and MariaDB vectors: see capabilities

docs.title: migrate
docs.text: The migration engine: migrate.Engine with migrate.Engine.Diff, Plan, migrate.Engine.Apply, Status, Baseline, Drift, Resolve, Rehash, Inspect, AutoMigrate, Rollback and Rebase, plus migrate.ValidateOffline. A migration directory holds <version>_<name>.up.sql, optional hand-written .down.sql, snapshots and momo.sum. A database implements migrate.Dialect; the implementations are migrate/postgres, migrate/sqlite and migrate/mysql, and migrate/migratetest holds helpers for tests. Which of them the momo migrate command runs is generated in capabilities; the others are library APIs. See migrations.

docs.title: gen
docs.text:
The generator. gen.Load reads model packages into a gen.Graph, gen.Emit writes the generated files through the Writer, which is the only file writer (it refuses targets that are not generated, formats the output and is deterministic). gen.Plugin is the extension interface. Generated Go files start with // Code generated by momo (format 1). DO NOT EDIT.; the header carries the format number and no release version.

Package Purpose gen/config momo.yaml parsing, shared with the CLI gen/fromdb models from a PostgreSQL database (momo generate --from-db) gen/viz Mermaid and DOT diagrams (momo viz), also a gen.Plugin gen/apiquery cursor, limit and filter helpers for generated APIs gen/graphql GraphQL SDL, gqlgen glue and config, a gen.Plugin gen/grpc .proto, lock and gRPC servers, a gen.Plugin gen/openapi OpenAPI 3.1 document and handlers, a gen.Plugin gen/naming, gen/tags, gen/typemap naming presets, tag parsing, Go type to SQL type

docs.title: Other packages
docs.text:
• cli: the CLI as a library (generate, migrate, viz, help). cli.Main(plugins...) builds a momo binary with your own generator plugins; cmd/momo is a thin caller of it with the built-in graphql, grpc, openapi and viz plugins.
  • momovet and cmd/momovet: the analyzer for non-constant raw SQL; see momovet.
  • momotest: a schema or a rolled-back transaction per test with your migrations applied; momotest/sqlitetest is the SQLite variant, kept apart so PostgreSQL tests do not link cgo. See testing.
  • momolog: a log/slog hook for statements and relation loads.
  • obs: ready-made Hook and RelationHook implementations (a recorder and an N+1 relation-load detector); imports only momo. See observability.
  • importer, importer/{gorm,bun,ent}: static readers of other ORMs' models; see importers.
  • bench is a separate Go module with the comparison benchmarks; see performance.

docs.title: Test layout
docs.text: Database tests carry the integration build tag, so the default go test run needs no database. internal/testdb returns connection strings for a per-test schema or database, and internal/testdb/testopen opens a *momo.DB per dialect, with testopen.Each running a test once per dialect available in the build. CI sets MOMO_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1, which turns a missing database URL from a skip into a failure. Shared feature suites live in internal/suite. See contributing for the commands.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Budgets are measured, never aspirational. This page starts with the hook overhead budget that TestSelectNoHooksAllocBudget enforces. The bench/ module (a separate Go module, so GORM, Ent and Bun never enter the library's import graph) holds the comparison workloads; its methodology, versions and regression policy are added here as the suite lands.

docs.title: Hook overhead budget
docs.text:
A primary-key lookup on a database with no hooks registered must not allocate more than the budget below. The figure is allocs/op of BenchmarkSelectNoHooks, measured by the TestSelectNoHooksAllocBudget run in CI. The full CI matrix (Go 1.26 and 1.27, PostgreSQL 16 and 17 with pgvector 0.8.7) measures the same 32, so one budget covers every combination. The test fails when the measured value rises above the budget, so an allocation added to the disabled-hook path is caught. Lower the budget in the same change whenever the path gets cheaper.

Benchmark Budget BenchmarkSelectNoHooks allocs/op 32

To reproduce, run make db-up, then make bench-hooks. The benchmark opens a database, so it only compiles with the integration build tag and make bench-smoke skips it; the bench-module CI job runs make bench-hooks against the pgvector service.

docs.title: Streaming memory bound
docs.text:
SelectQuery.Each hands rows to a callback one at a time and must not buffer the result set. TestStreamingBoundedMemory iterates one million rows with Each, reads the heap after a forced collection every 100000 rows, and fails when the heap has grown by more than the bound below, so an Each that collects the rows first is caught.

Limit Value Streaming heap growth bound (MiB) 16

docs.title: Comparison suite
docs.text: The bench/ module compares Momo with handwritten pgx and database/sql, GORM, Ent and Bun on one PostgreSQL server. Every operation is defined once in bench/workload and each library implements it in bench/adapters; the equivalence test TestBenchEquivalence fails when an adapter returns different rows than the handwritten pgx reference or leaves different state after a write, so a workload whose SQL meaning differs between libraries cannot be published.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Identical pool settings for every adapter: 16 connections, one hour connection lifetime. The native pgx path uses the statement cache; the other libraries run on the pgx standard library driver.
  • GORM runs with SkipDefaultTransaction, as Momo adds no implicit transaction. Bun runs on the same pgx standard library database/sql handle as Ent and GORM, so the comparison isolates the ORM layer. No library cache is enabled.
  • The data is deterministic: a fixed seed, 200 customers with 5 orders each. ANALYZE runs after seeding.
  • ORM-only microbenchmarks report p50, p95 and p99 per call beside allocations, for six operations over all six libraries. A mixed read and write workload with concurrency and the bulk insert paths have their own runners.
  • Bulk insert compares chunked VALUES, COPY and Momo's Unnest, one statement with one array parameter per column, at 1000, 10000 and 40000 rows.
  • Vector search is compared at equal recall: a sweep picks the smallest hnsw.ef_search whose recall at 10 reaches 0.95 against exact search, and both the Momo builder and the handwritten statement then run at that setting.
  • Generated-code size and compile cost of the benchmark models are measured by bench/codesize.

docs.title: Pinned versions
docs.text: The module versions are pinned in bench/go.mod; each run records them in versions.txt and env.json, together with the Go toolchain, the machine, the PostgreSQL version and the pgvector version. The database image is pgvector/pgvector:0.8.7-pg17.

docs.title: Reproducing a run
docs.text: make db-up starts PostgreSQL with pgvector. Then make bench runs the whole suite ten times per benchmark and writes bench/results/ under a directory named by UTC time, operating system and architecture, with env.json, versions.txt, codesize.json, raw.txt and summary.txt, plus vector-encoding.txt (the BenchmarkVectorEncoding run of text against binary pgx vector codecs) when a database is configured. make bench-suite-smoke runs one iteration of everything and is what CI uses. make bench-generate regenerates the Momo metadata and the Ent client.

docs.title: Regression policy
docs.text:
• Timings are judged only on a dedicated machine: a regression is flagged when benchstat reports a change above 10 percent with p below 0.05 across two consecutive full runs. Shared CI runners are too noisy for timings, so CI never gates on them.
  • Allocation counts are deterministic, so CI gates them: the bench-module job of ci.yml and ci-agent.yml runs make bench-gate, which runs the allocation benchmarks, compares allocs/op with bench/baseline/allocs.txt using benchstat and fails above 5 percent with p below 0.05. The gate runs in that one job only, against the PostgreSQL service the job already starts, so a pull request pays for one database job and not a second one. The recipe runs under bash with pipefail, and benchgate exits 2 (never 0) when the new run has no allocs/op rows or lacks a benchmark that the baseline has, so a run that never happened cannot pass. make bench-gate runs the same comparison locally and make bench-baseline rewrites the baseline.
  • Budgets are the median of the reference run plus 10 percent and are reviewed on every full run.

docs.title: Status of the published numbers
docs.text: No full run on a dedicated machine has been committed yet, so this page records no comparative timings. The only budget in force is the hook overhead budget above, which CI enforces. Timing figures will be added from the stored bench/results/ run, never from a shared runner.

docs.title: Interceptors: application-level statement rules
docs.text: An interceptor is a function attached to one *momo.DB handle with momo.WithInterceptor. It runs before the typed statements of that handle, may append predicates to them, and may deny them by returning an error. It is an application-level guard, not a privacy or security boundary: it filters only the primary table of the typed Select, Insert, Upsert, Update, SoftDelete and Delete builders, and every path listed under "What an interceptor does not cover" bypasses it. Use it to remove accidents, and use database row-level security where isolation must hold when application code is wrong.

docs.title: What an interceptor sees
docs.text:
type Operation struct {
    Kind  string      // "select", "insert", "upsert", "update", "delete", "truncate"
    Table string
    Where []Predicate // starts empty; append to it
}

type Interceptor func(ctx context.Context, op *Operation) error
  • Select, update and delete: the predicates in Where are ANDed to the statement and appear in the SQL that SQL returns and that the hooks see.
  • Insert and upsert: the interceptor runs so it can deny the statement; predicates appended to them are ignored. It runs when the statement executes (Exec, Rows), never for SQL, which for an insert runs neither interceptors nor hooks.
  • An Upsert, or an Insert with OnConflict and DoUpdate, has the kind upsert, not insert. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE can overwrite an existing row, including a row of another tenant that shares the conflict key, and an appended predicate cannot stop it. A tenant rule must therefore deny the kind upsert or constrain it by other means (see the recipe). An Insert with DoNothing is an insert.
  • A soft delete has the kind delete.
  • Truncate has the kind truncate. It removes every row of the table, so a tenant-scoped handle should deny it; a predicate appended to it is ignored.
  • BulkUpdate is an update and keeps the predicates. Merge is an upsert when it has a matched update and an insert otherwise; a predicate an interceptor appends makes it fail with ErrValidation, because it cannot be applied without changing which rows match. InsertQuery.Copy is an insert (deny only).
  • Interceptors run in registration order, before the typed model hooks (Meta.Hooks), so a denied statement never reaches a Before hook. The first error stops the chain and the statement; it is returned as a momo.Error of kind ErrValidation that still reaches the interceptor's own error with errors.Is. No SQL runs.
  • The predicates an interceptor adds are not a caller filter: an update or delete with no Where of its own is still refused with ErrUnfilteredMutation unless AllRows confirms it. A version-checked model update whose row is hidden by an interceptor predicate returns ErrNotFound, not ErrOptimisticLock. The count that decides between the two is a select, so your select interceptors run for it too.

docs.title: The context
docs.text: Interceptors receive the statement's context, so a tenant usually comes from ctx. SQL, which has no context argument, runs the interceptors with context.Background. An interceptor that reads the tenant from ctx sees none there: the SQL it returns shows no tenant predicate, and an interceptor that denies when the tenant is missing denies every SQL call. Inspect the statement a handle really runs through the hook events, or give the handle its tenant at construction (below) so the predicate does not depend on ctx.

docs.title: Recipe: a tenant handle
docs.text:
Build one handle per tenant (or per request) and give it the tenant predicate. The tenant comes from the handle's own configuration, so a statement cannot choose another one.

func tenantDB(drv momo.Driver, tenantID int64) *momo.DB {
    return momo.New(drv, momo.WithInterceptor(func(ctx context.Context, op *momo.Operation) error {
        if op.Table != "documents" {
            return nil
        }
        switch op.Kind {
        case "select", "update", "delete":
            op.Where = append(op.Where, DocTenantID.Eq(tenantID))
        case "upsert":
            return errors.New("upsert is not allowed on a tenant handle")
        case "truncate":
            return errors.New("truncate is not allowed on a tenant handle")
        }
        return nil
    }))
}

Inserts are not filtered by a predicate: the tenant column of a new row is the model's own value, so set it in a BeforeInsert model method (func (m *Model) BeforeInsert(ctx context.Context) error, wired into Meta.Hooks by momo generate) and do not trust the caller to set it. BeforeInsert runs only for Model and Models inserts: InsertQuery.Values, ValuesRows and FromSelect inserts have no model and skip it, so a tenant handle that relies on the hook must also deny those forms, or deny inserts altogether and write through a trusted handle.

A read-only handle denies every write:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"

    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
)

func readOnly(drv momo.Driver) *momo.DB {
    return momo.New(drv, momo.WithInterceptor(func(ctx context.Context, op *momo.Operation) error {
        if op.Kind != "select" {
            return fmt.Errorf("handle is read-only: %s on %s", op.Kind, op.Table)
        }
        return nil
    }))
}

func main() { _ = readOnly }

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
An interceptor belongs to the handle it was registered on:

  • A transaction begun with Begin or Tx from that handle runs the same interceptors.
  • A handle created by another call to momo.New, even over the same driver, has none of them.
  • Registering an interceptor on one handle never changes another.

docs.title: What an interceptor does not cover
docs.text:
Each of these bypasses every interceptor. Scope them explicitly or use row-level security.

  • Relation loading: Load, Preload and LoadCounts query the related tables without interceptors.
  • Joined relation tables: for a Joined relation only the primary table is filtered; the joined table is not.
  • The association helpers (Link, Unlink, Replace and the like) and graph creation.
  • Subqueries and other sources rendered inside a statement: subquery operands, UPDATE ... FROM sources, and the FromSelect source of an insert.
  • Raw SQL of every kind: momo.Exec, momo.MapRows, momo.Scalars, momo.Query, momo.QueryRows, momo.SQL fragments and momo.RawSubquery.
  • Bulk loading with COPY: InsertQuery[T].Copy runs the insert interceptors (deny only) and BeforeInsert, but a predicate an interceptor adds is ignored, and momo.CopierOf(...).CopyFrom skips them entirely.
  • Anything run on the driver directly, and any other *momo.DB over the same driver.

For isolation that holds even when application code is wrong, use database row-level security with the transaction setup hook (WithTxSetup) and a policy on the table. Treat interceptors as the first layer and row-level security as the enforcing one.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Sensitive columns are masked in hook events: bound values of columns tagged sensitive reach hooks as momo.RedactedArg.
  • Typed model hooks (Meta.Hooks) change values on a model before a write and after a read; momo generate fills them from model methods named BeforeInsert, BeforeUpdate, BeforeDelete and AfterLoad with the signature func(context.Context) error, so there is nothing to set by hand; see the HookSet documentation for the semantics and for what a Before hook may leave behind when a statement then fails.

docs.title: Go to SQL type mapping
docs.text: This page lists which SQL column type Momo uses for each Go field type, what survives a round trip, and where the edges are. The tables are checked by tests: TestTypeMappingDoc fails when a row here disagrees with the generator's type map or a codec's SQLType, and TestTypeMapping creates a column of each documented PostgreSQL type on a live server, and the generated SQLite type on a live SQLite database, and round-trips edge values through it.

docs.title: How a type is chosen
docs.text:
1. A field whose type implements the codec contract (types.Codec: Scan, Value and SQLType) uses its own SQLType. This is how types.TimeOfDay and types.Hstore get their columns.
  2. Otherwise the generator maps the Go type with its built-in table (package gen/typemap). A pointer and the sql.Null* wrappers map like the type they wrap: nullability is a column property, not a type property.
  3. A Go type with no mapping (for example uint64 or map) makes typemap.Map return an error wrapping momo.ErrUnsupported, which the generator reports at the field. Give the type a codec or declare the column yourself.

docs.title: Generated mappings
docs.text:
N is the size tag for string and the dim tag for vector types. A vector.Vector or vector.HalfVector field without dim is supported: it maps to the bare vector or halfvec type, a dimensionless column that holds embeddings of any size (see vectors.md). vector.SparseVector and vector.Bits require dim. SQLite has no vector types. A slice of a scalar maps to the PostgreSQL array of its element type; SQLite has no array columns, so the generator rejects them there.

Go type PostgreSQL SQLite MySQL int bigint INTEGER unsupported int8 smallint INTEGER unsupported int16 smallint INTEGER unsupported int32 integer INTEGER unsupported int64 bigint INTEGER unsupported float32 real REAL unsupported float64 double precision REAL unsupported bool boolean INTEGER unsupported string text TEXT unsupported string with size:N character varying(N) TEXT unsupported []byte bytea BLOB unsupported time.Time timestamp with time zone TEXT unsupported types.UUID uuid TEXT unsupported uuid.UUID (github.com/google/uuid) uuid TEXT unsupported types.Date date TEXT unsupported types.JSON[T] jsonb TEXT unsupported vector.Vector vector(N) unsupported unsupported vector.HalfVector halfvec(N) unsupported unsupported vector.SparseVector sparsevec(N) unsupported unsupported vector.Bits bit(N) unsupported unsupported vector.Vector (no dim) vector unsupported unsupported vector.HalfVector (no dim) halfvec unsupported unsupported []string text[] unsupported unsupported []int16 smallint[] unsupported unsupported []int32 integer[] unsupported unsupported []int64 bigint[] unsupported unsupported []bool boolean[] unsupported unsupported []float32 real[] unsupported unsupported []float64 double precision[] unsupported unsupported []types.UUID uuid[] unsupported unsupported []uuid.UUID (github.com/google/uuid) uuid[] unsupported unsupported

The MySQL column is what typemap.Map returns for MySQL: the generator emits no MySQL models, so every Go type shows unsupported there until it does. Only an error that wraps momo.ErrUnsupported shows as unsupported; any other error from typemap.Map fails the generation of this table.

The PostgreSQL type of time.Time can be changed for the whole project with the types: section of momo.yaml, for example types: {time.Time: timestamp(3)} for a database created by Prisma (see naming: prisma in ai-guide.md). Only time.Time can be overridden; a type: tag on a field still wins, and SQLite ignores the setting. timestamp(3) stores a wall clock without a zone, so follow the timestamp notes below and pass UTC times.

On SQLite, bool is stored as 0 or 1, and time.Time, types.UUID, types.Date and types.JSON[T] are stored as text. The SQLite column is what the generator emits. The SQLite driver (driver/sqlitedriver, cgo, not on Windows) reads text columns back into time.Time, *time.Time, sql.NullTime, sql.Null[time.Time] and types.Date, whatever the column was declared as.

docs.title: Codec-provided mappings
docs.text:
These types are not in the generator's table. Their own SQLType method names the column; the generator's table is the fallback for everything else.

Go type PostgreSQL SQLite types.TimeOfDay time TEXT types.Hstore hstore TEXT types.TSVector tsvector TEXT types.TSQuery tsquery TEXT

types.Hstore needs the hstore extension; the vector types need vector (pgvector). Momo never runs CREATE EXTENSION for you.

docs.title: Mappings you declare yourself
docs.text:
The generator never emits these columns, but the Go types work against them when you write the DDL (or a migration) by hand. There is no SQLite column to document because nothing generates one.

Go type PostgreSQL SQLite time.Time (timestamp) timestamp n/a string (decimal) numeric n/a

docs.title: Edge values and behavior
docs.text:
Each statement below is asserted by a test against PostgreSQL. The generated SQLite column of every row is also round-tripped on a live SQLite database, except NaN, which SQLite does not have (see Floats).

  • Integers: math.MaxInt64 and math.MinInt64 round-trip through bigint; int is 64-bit and maps to bigint. A value that does not fit the column (an int64 above math.MaxInt16 into smallint) is a database error, not a silent truncation. uint64 has no mapping and is rejected when bound if it exceeds math.MaxInt64.
  • Floats: NaN, +Inf and -Inf are legal double precision and real values and round-trip. Compare with math.IsNaN, since NaN != NaN. SQLite has no NaN: binding a float32 or float64 NaN (or a pointer to one) is ErrValidation and nothing is stored, rather than a silent NULL. +Inf and -Inf are legal REAL values.
  • Strings: any valid UTF-8 round-trips, including quotes and backslashes (they are bound, never interpolated). PostgreSQL rejects U+0000 in text. A string longer than size is a database error on character varying(N).
  • []byte: nil stores NULL; an empty non-nil slice stores an empty bytea.
  • time.Time on timestamptz: the instant is preserved, the zone is not. A value written at +05:30 reads back as the same instant in the server session's location, so compare with Time.Equal, not ==. Precision is microseconds; finer digits are cut. Times before 1970 and year 9999 work.
  • time.Time on timestamp (no zone): you store a wall clock. Pass t.UTC() and treat the column as UTC; a value in another zone is stored as its UTC wall clock.
  • types.Date: stores the year, month and day of Time in its own location; it reads back at midnight UTC. Compare the date, not the zone.
  • types.UUID: round-trips all 16 bytes, including the all-zero UUID.
  • types.JSON[T]: encodes with encoding/json. An empty slice and a nil slice are different JSON ([] and null) and read back as such. Query it with jsonop.Text, jsonop.Path, jsonop.Contains and jsonop.HasKey (package github.com/azrtydxb/momo/jsonop). A nullable column holds either SQL NULL or the JSON literal null; an extraction is NULL for both and for a missing key, so test the column itself with IsNull. Grouping by an extraction works only for plain keys (letters, digits, underscore) and not on a sensitive column; see the AI guide pitfalls.
  • types.TimeOfDay: nanoseconds since midnight, truncated to microseconds (PostgreSQL time precision); 86399999999000 is the last representable value, and a value outside one day is an error.
  • types.Hstore: a nil *string value is an hstore NULL; keys and values with quotes and backslashes are escaped.
  • types.TSVector and types.TSQuery: the server's text form, with the lexemes sorted and normalized, so write values in that canonical form to compare them with ==. An empty tsvector reads back empty. Full-text expressions are PostgreSQL only (see docs/fulltext.md).
  • []string on text[]: elements containing commas, quotes, the text NULL, or empty strings round-trip; an empty slice reads back empty.
  • Slices as arrays: only []string, []int16, []int32, []int64, []bool, []float32, []float64 and []types.UUID (uuid[]) map, and so does a []uuid.UUID from github.com/google/uuid (see the next item). []int is not mapped, because its width is platform dependent; use []int64. []string with a size tag becomes character varying(N)[]. A nil slice binds as NULL, so inserting it into a NOT NULL array column fails with a not-null violation; pass an empty non-nil slice (it stores {}), or give the column a default '{}' and omit it. The array predicates bind a nil value list as an empty array, never NULL.
  • uuid.UUID, *uuid.UUID and []uuid.UUID from github.com/google/uuid map to uuid and uuid[] on PostgreSQL and uuid.UUID to TEXT on SQLite (canonical text; []uuid.UUID has no SQLite column), with no type: tag. MySQL has no uuid mapping, as for types.UUID. The generator recognizes the type by its import path and adds no dependency to momo; your module requires github.com/google/uuid only when your models import it. --from-db writes these types with introspect.uuid: google. A named type over uuid.UUID (type ID uuid.UUID) is not mapped: give the field type:uuid. A UUID type of another package is not mapped either.
  • Decimal: carry numeric as a string to avoid binary floating point. Values beyond float64 precision round-trip exactly, and numeric also accepts NaN.

docs.title: Null handling
docs.text: A column that can be NULL needs a Go type that can hold NULL: a pointer (*int64), a sql.Null* wrapper, or a type whose Scan accepts nil. Scanning NULL into a plain int64 or into a codec from the types package is an error, never a silent zero value.

docs.title: Using these docs with an AI coding agent
docs.text: Momo is meant to be written by agents as well as people. The documentation is built so an agent can read it without scraping HTML.

docs.title: Where an agent should read
docs.text:
• Agent guide: one self-contained file with setup, modeling, migrations, queries, relations, vectors, errors, testing and the rules. If an agent reads one page, it reads this one.
  • llms.txt on the documentation site lists every page with a link to its raw Markdown. llms-full.txt contains the Markdown of every page in one file. Each page also has a raw .md twin next to its HTML. All three are generated at build time and exist under every published version of the site.
  • The repository root has its own llms.txt for agents that read the repository instead of the site.

docs.title: Canonical patterns
docs.text:
The shapes below are the ones the guide teaches. The linked examples run against PostgreSQL in CI.

  • Describe a table as a struct that embeds momo.Model, run momo generate, and build queries from the generated descriptors. See getting started and the quickstart example.
  • Insert with Insert[T] and Model, read with Select[T] and Where, change rows with Update[T] and Set, remove them with Delete[T] or SoftDelete. See crud-zero-null.
  • Run related statements in db.Tx and use the tx it passes in. See transactions.
  • Load relations explicitly with Load, LoadAll or Preload. See relations.
  • Change a schema by editing the model and running momo migrate diff, then review the SQL it wrote. See migrations.

docs.title: AGENTS.md snippet
docs.text:
Copy the block below into the AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md) of a repository that uses Momo. It is the short form of the rules in section 12 of the agent guide; a test keeps it complete.

## Momo (Go ORM)

- PostgreSQL with pgvector is the reference database. The generated status in docs/capabilities.md lists the other databases and the dialects `momo migrate` runs; check it before relying on a feature there.
- Run `momo generate` after every model change and commit the generated files. Never edit generated files.
- A non-pointer model field is NOT NULL; a pointer field is nullable.
- Pass user input only as arguments to `momo.SQL`, `momo.TypedSQL`, `momo.Exec`, `momo.Scalars`, `momo.Query` and `momo.QueryRows`. Never build SQL by string concatenation.
- Never bypass `ErrUnfilteredMutation` with `AllRows`; add a `Where`.
- Check errors with `errors.Is` against the `momo.Err*` sentinels. Never match error text.
- Use only the `tx` handle inside `db.Tx`. Retry the whole transaction on `ErrSerialization`, never inside it.
- Never edit a migration that has been applied. Write a new one with `momo migrate diff`.
- Run `momo generate --check` in CI.
- Run `momo migrate validate` in CI.
- Test against a real PostgreSQL with pgvector. Do not mock `momo.Querier`.
- Full reference: https://azrtydxb.github.io/momo/latest/ai-guide.md

docs.title: Momo guide for AI coding agents
docs.text:
Target: github.com/azrtydxb/momo v0.6.0. Read this file instead of the Momo source. Every identifier below was checked against v0.6.0. Where the guide says DON'T, the call either fails, silently does the wrong thing, or is a known bug.

Imports used throughout:

import (
    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo"                    // core: DB, Tx, Select, Insert, Update, Delete, errors
    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"   // PostgreSQL driver (pgx v5)
    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo/vector"             // vector.Vector, HalfVector, SparseVector, Bits
    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo/types"              // types.UUID, Date, JSON[T], TimeOfDay, Hstore, TSVector, TSQuery
    "yourmodule/models"                           // your structs
    "yourmodule/models/task"                      // GENERATED: one package per model (lowercase model name)
)

Deeper docs: README, relations, migrations, vectors, capabilities, supported versions, type mapping, architecture, examples.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
• v0.6.0 supports PostgreSQL 16 and 17 with pgvector 0.8.x, through pgx v5; the other databases are in the status block below.

Database status:

A database is usable when a driver package for it exists under driver/:

  • PostgreSQL: usable through driver/pgxdriver (vector builders: yes). Migrations: migrate/postgres, run by momo migrate.
  • SQLite: usable through driver/sqlitedriver (needs cgo, not on Windows, vector builders: yes) and driver/sqlitepure (vector builders: no). Migrations: migrate/sqlite, library only (momo migrate does not select it).
  • MySQL and MariaDB: usable through driver/mysqldriver (vector storage and builders depend on the server version). Migrations: migrate/mysql, library only (momo migrate does not select it).
  • PostgreSQL is the reference database. Check the dialect columns of docs/capabilities.md before relying on a feature on another database. Keep dialects: at [postgres] for generated migrations. momo migrate exits 2 for a dialect it does not link; library migrations go through migrate.NewEngine.
  • Go 1.26.10 or newer (the go.mod floor, which carries the standard-library security fixes). Pre-v1: no compatibility promise; pin the exact version.
  • diff writes forward migrations only. momo migrate rollback [--group] runs a hand-written .down.sql, momo migrate lint reports risky operations, and momo migrate rebase --onto <dir> regenerates a branch's migrations on a target's.
  • momo generate --from-db DATABASE_URL turns a live PostgreSQL database into models and an init snapshot (see migrations). Other databases: write models by hand.
  • Reciprocal-rank-fusion hybrid search is momo.HybridSearch (PostgreSQL only, see vectors.md). Full-text search (types.TSVector, fts.Match, fts.RankCD, fts.Headline, the query builders) exists on PostgreSQL; to weigh the signals yourself, combine a vector distance with a text rank in one score as shown in fulltext.md.

Details: capabilities.md. Example: quickstart.

docs.title: 2. Install and tooling
docs.text:
go get github.com/azrtydxb/momo@v0.6.0                # adds the library to go.mod and writes go.sum
go install github.com/azrtydxb/momo/cmd/momo@v0.6.0   # the CLI: generate, migrate, import, viz, help

Run go get first in a fresh module: it produces go.sum, which go run and the generated code's compilation need. go install puts momo in $(go env GOPATH)/bin; make sure that is on PATH.

Layout of a project (the models package holds structs; momo generate writes into it):

go.mod
momo.yaml
models/models.go          # yours
models/momo_gen.go        # generated (MomoMeta for each model). Commit it.
models/task/momo_gen.go   # generated: columns and relations of Task. Commit it.
migrations/               # momo migrate diff writes here. Commit it.

Minimal momo.yaml (at the module root; the CLI finds it by walking up to go.mod):

version: 1
packages:
  - ./models
dialects: [postgres]
migrate:
  dir:
    postgres: migrations
  url_env:
    postgres: DATABASE_URL

naming: is optional: momo (default: snake_case columns, plural snake_case tables), gorm, bun, ent, prisma. Pick one and never change it: a change renames columns.

naming: prisma matches a database that Prisma created: the table is the model name as written and quoted (KbChunk), the column is camelCase (createdAt, accountId; an ID word at the end becomes Id, and a trailing IDs becomes Ids, so UserIDs is userIds), and the constraint and index names are <Table>_pkey, <Table>_<col>_fkey, <Table>_<col>_key (unique) and <Table>_<col>_idx. Those names come out of the table and column names, so no tag is needed for single-column keys and indexes.

Limits of the preset:

  • A composite @@index or @@unique is named by Prisma from all its columns (<Table>_<a>_<b>_idx). Name such an index explicitly in MomoConfig or with an index:/unique: tag name.
  • The implicit many-to-many table is named _AToB (model names in alphabetical order), but its A and B columns and its foreign key names are not reproduced. Declare that table with an explicit join model instead.
  • A column name that does not follow the camelCase rule needs a column: tag.

Prisma maps DateTime to timestamp(3), so add a types: section:

naming: prisma
types:
  time.Time: timestamp(3)

types: overrides the default PostgreSQL column type of a Go type. Only time.Time is supported, and the value must be timestamp, timestamptz, time or timetz with an optional precision 0-6 and an optional with/without time zone (anything else is refused, as it is written into DDL). A type: tag on a field still wins. It applies when the first entry of dialects is PostgreSQL (or dialects is empty); with SQLite first it is ignored. Without it time.Time is timestamp with time zone.

Generate:

//go:generate momo generate

momo generate            # writes *_gen.go
momo generate --check    # CI: exit 1 and "stale: <path>" lines when stale; writes nothing

Rules:

  • DO run momo generate after every change to a model struct or tag, before compiling code that uses the generated packages.
  • DO commit generated files. DON'T edit *_gen.go and DON'T name your own files *_gen.go (the generator refuses to overwrite non-generated files).
  • DO put *_gen.go text eol=lf in .gitattributes if anyone uses Windows, to keep checkouts byte-identical (--check already treats a CRLF copy as current).
  • DON'T use go run of the CLI inside app code; the library (momo) never imports the generator.

Details: README "Configure and generate". Example: quickstart.

docs.title: 3. Connecting
docs.text:
func openDB(ctx context.Context, url string) (*momo.DB, func(), error) {
    pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, url) // (ctx, string) (*pgxpool.Pool, error)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    return momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool)), pool.Close, nil // New(pool, opts ...Option) momo.Driver
}
  • The caller owns and closes the pool. momo.DB has no Close.
  • *momo.DB is safe for concurrent use; create one at startup and share it.
  • DSN: postgres://user:password@host:5432/dbname?sslmode=verify-full. Use sslmode=disable for local development only. Momo adds no TLS options; pgx reads sslmode, sslrootcert, ... from the URL.
  • Read the URL from the environment, never hard-code credentials.
  • Pool sizing: Momo documents no recommendation and sets nothing. pgxpool options (for example pool_max_conns=N in the URL) apply. Each open Tx, vecsearch.With block, Replace and CreateGraph holds one connection for its whole duration.

Other constructors:

sqlDB, drv := pgxdriver.FromConnConfig(cfg, opts...) // cfg *pgx.ConnConfig; returns (*sql.DB, momo.Driver)
drv = pgxdriver.FromSQLDB(sqlDB)                     // sqlDB must be backed by pgx stdlib; for an existing *sql.Tx see SQLTx, AdoptTx and UnwrapSQLTx in section Transactions

database/sql paths have no Batch or COPY path (relation loading falls back to sequential statements; correct, just slower).

PgBouncer (transaction pooling):

  • pgxdriver.New defaults to pgx.QueryExecModeExec (unnamed statements, server-side binding). That is PgBouncer-safe; set nothing.
  • That mode sends no parameter types, so the driver converts what pgx cannot encode. []uuid.UUID (github.com/google/uuid), []types.UUID and any slice of a [16]byte type that implements fmt.Stringer bind to id = ANY(?::uuid[]) (with or without the cast; a nil slice is NULL). A raw []byte is bytea text and a jsonb column rejects it: pass the JSON as json.RawMessage or string, or use types.JSON[T]. The pgxdriver tests TestUUIDSliceBindsToAnyArray and TestJSONBBinding pin this.
  • pgxdriver.WithExecMode(m) accepts pgx.QueryExecModeCacheStatement, pgx.QueryExecModeCacheDescribe, pgx.QueryExecModeDescribeExec (import github.com/jackc/pgx/v5; not tested through PgBouncer). The simple protocol is rejected with ErrUnsupported on every query. DON'T select it.
  • With FromConnConfig set cfg.DefaultQueryExecMode = pgx.QueryExecModeExec first; pgx defaults to CacheStatement, which is NOT PgBouncer-safe. Its opts have no effect.
  • DON'T run momo migrate through a transaction pooler (section 5).
  • Set search_path per role or per transaction, not at connection startup.

Details: capabilities.md "Getting connected", supported-versions.md "PgBouncer".

docs.title: 4. Modeling
docs.text:
A model is a struct that embeds momo.Model BY VALUE. The tag on that embedded field names the table. The tag grammar is momo:"opt,opt:value,..."; a value cannot contain a comma. An unknown, duplicate or malformed option is a generator diagnostic and nothing is written for that package.

type Account struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:accounts"`
    ID         int64      `momo:"pk,identity"`
    Email      string     `momo:"size:200,unique"`
    Plan       string     `momo:"size:20,default:'free',index"`
    Note       *string    `momo:"size:500"`                         // pointer = nullable
    Balance    int64      `momo:"default:0"`
    Version    int64      `momo:"version,default:0"`                // optimistic lock
    CreatedAt  time.Time  `momo:"column:created_at,created_at"`     // set by Momo on insert
    UpdatedAt  time.Time  `momo:"column:updated_at,updated_at"`     // set by Momo on update
    DeletedAt  *time.Time `momo:"column:deleted_at,soft_delete:timestamp"`
    Embedding  vector.Vector `momo:"dim:1536"`                      // pgvector column

    Posts []Post `momo:"has_many,fk:AccountID"`
}

Nullability and column rules:

  • A non-pointer Go field is NOT NULL. A pointer (*string), a sql.Null* type, or the nullable tag makes the column nullable. notnull is redundant for non-pointers and a diagnostic on pointers.
  • A nullable field generates momo.NullColumn[T] (has SetNull()); a non-nullable one generates momo.Column[T] (SetNull() does not compile).
  • A primary key must not be nullable.
  • Scanning NULL into a non-pointer field is an error. Use pointers for nullable columns.
  • Go type to column type: see TYPE_MAPPING.md (int is bigint, string is text, string with size:N is varchar(N), time.Time is timestamptz, types.UUID is uuid, types.JSON[T] is jsonb). uint64, maps and unknown types have no mapping: add type:<sql> or a codec.
  • JSON columns: jsonop.Text, jsonop.Path, jsonop.Contains and jsonop.HasKey (package github.com/azrtydxb/momo/jsonop) are typed operators over a types.JSON[T] column; the extractions are string expressions usable in Where, OrderBy and Columns. An extraction is NULL for a missing key and for JSON null alike, a SQL NULL column is tested with IsNull on the column, and the JSON literal null is matched by comparing the column with a types.JSON whose value is nil. jsonop.HasKey is true for a key whose value is JSON null. A numeric key in jsonop.Text or jsonop.HasKey is an object key; only jsonop.Path elements made of digits can be array indexes. SQLite renders json_extract and json_type (jsonop.Contains is ErrUnsupported there); MySQL renders its JSON functions.
  • Column names default to the naming preset (CreatedAt becomes created_at). Fields are exported only; a tag on an unexported field is a diagnostic. Skip a field with momo:"-".

Tag reference (all lower case):

Tag Meaning table:<name> (on momo.Model) table name; always set it. Also schema:<name>. pk primary key; several pk fields make a composite key, declared in field order unless Config.PrimaryKey lists the fields in another order (a tag belongs_to target needs a single-column key) identity, identity:always database-generated identity (GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY; identity:always is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, so a client-supplied value is refused by the database; not on MySQL) serial PostgreSQL smallserial/serial/bigserial id by Go int width (sequence owned by the column, DEFAULT nextval); omitted from inserts and read back with RETURNING like identity; excludes identity and default; refused on other dialects column:<name> column name size:<n> varchar(n); strings only precision:<p>, scale:<s> numeric precision (float, decimal, or a string without size that carries a numeric); scale needs precision dim:<n> vector dimension; optional on vector and halfvec (none: dimensionless column), required on sparsevec and bit, invalid elsewhere default:<sql> column default, raw SQL (default:now(), default:'free', default:0) unique / unique:<name> unique index (single column) index / index:<name> index; modifiers sort:asc\|desc, nulls:first\|last, method:<m> need index or unique idgen:<name> client-generated string id (cuid, uuid, ulid or a name registered with WithIDGenerator); filled on insert when the field is empty dbdefault leave the column to the database default while the field holds its zero value: a Model/Models insert omits it and reads the stored value back (see Database defaults) version optimistic-lock column (integer type) created_at[:unix\|unixmilli\|unixnano], updated_at automatic timestamps; field type time.Time, *time.Time, int64 or *int64 soft_delete:timestamp\|unix\|bool soft-delete marker; Go type *time.Time, *int64 or bool read_only, create_only, immutable write permissions: never written; written on insert only; never updated sensitive excluded from the generated ColumnByName allowlist (use for secrets) type:<sql>, collate:<c>, check:<expr>, comment:<t>, enum:<name> raw column type, collation, check, comment, enum type embedded, prefix:<p> flatten a named struct-typed field into this table (anonymous embedded structs flatten by themselves); prefix prepends to its column names nullable, notnull explicit nullability (rarely needed)

MomoConfig for what tags cannot express: composite or partial indexes, vector indexes, checks, enums, views, triggers, policies. The generator reads this method statically and never runs it; arguments are &receiver.Field pointers and string literals only.

func (a *Account) MomoConfig(c *momo.Config) {
    c.Unique("accounts_email_plan_key", &a.Email, &a.Plan)
    c.Index("accounts_plan_live_idx", &a.Plan).Where("deleted_at IS NULL")
    c.Index("accounts_embedding_hnsw", &a.Embedding).
        Method("hnsw").
        Opclass(&a.Embedding, "vector_cosine_ops").
        With("m", "16").With("ef_construction", "64")
    c.Check("accounts_balance_nonneg", "balance >= 0")
}

An index name declared in MomoConfig must not collide with an auto-named <table>_<col>_idx produced by an index tag (the Plan field above already yields accounts_plan_idx); the generator refuses the duplicate.

Config methods: Config.Index, Config.IndexExpr, Config.Unique, Config.ForeignKey, Config.Check, Config.Enum, Config.Default, Config.Comment, Config.Collate, Config.IDGen, Config.FKName, Config.PrimaryKey, Config.View, Config.Function, Config.Trigger, Config.Policy, Config.RLS, Config.Partition, Config.PartitionOf. Index chain: IndexOpts.Unique() (on Config.Index or Config.IndexExpr), Where(pred), Method(m), IndexOpts.With(k, v), Opclass(field, op), Desc(field), Nulls(field, "first"|"last"), Concurrently() (diff writes the index as CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own no-transaction migration).

A unique expression index is Config.IndexExpr with IndexOpts.Unique(): c.IndexExpr("principal_email_key", "lower(email)").Unique(). Each string is one key: an expression, or the exact name of a column of the table, which is a plain column key, so c.IndexExpr("template_name_key", "company_id", "lower(name)").Unique() indexes (company_id, lower(name)). Add Where("deleted_at IS NULL") for a partial one. It is an index, not a constraint, so it cannot be a foreign key target. generate --from-db writes unique, mixed and partial expression indexes back this way; an expression key with DESC, NULLS or an operator class has no declaration.

A composite (multi-column) foreign key is declared in MomoConfig, not with a tag: c.ForeignKey("note_document_fk", []any{&n.CompanyID, &n.DocumentID}, "document", []string{"company_id", "id"}).OnDelete("CASCADE"). The first list holds &receiver.Field pointers, the table name and the referenced columns are string literals, and OnDelete/OnUpdate take CASCADE, RESTRICT, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT or NO ACTION. The referenced table must be the table of a model, and the referenced columns, in any order, must be its primary key, a unique constraint (c.Unique) or a non-partial unique index over plain columns; otherwise the generator reports a diagnostic. The key is a plain constraint: diff adds, replaces and drops it like a single-column key, and generate --from-db writes it back. There is no belongs_to form for a composite key; the relation still needs a single-column key.

Many-to-many needs join: with the same table on both models you declare it on (the reverse side is optional, but if declared it must carry join: too):

type Document struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:documents"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    Title      string
    Tags       []Tag `momo:"many2many,join:taggings"` // join table taggings(document_id, tag_id)
}

type Tag struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:tags"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    Name       string
    Documents  []Document `momo:"many2many,join:taggings"` // optional reverse side, same join table
}

Relation tags (a relation is an exported field of struct, slice or pointer type; it is not a column):

Tag Field type FK lives on Notes belongs_to,fk:<Field> *Target this struct fk names the FK field on THIS struct; make it a pointer if the relation is optional has_one,fk:<Field> *Target the target fk names the field on the TARGET has_many,fk:<Field> []Target the target fk names the field on the TARGET many2many,join:<table> []Target join table set join: (same table) on every side you declare; the reverse side is optional; two key columns <model>_<pkcol>

Extra relation options: polytype:<column> + polyvalue:<value> (both, on has_one/has_many only: polymorphic), on_delete: / on_update: (cascade, restrict, set_null, set_default, no_action; they affect only the FK emitted for belongs_to), no_constraint (emit no FK), fk_name:<name> (constraint name when not <table>_<col>_fkey; or Config.FKName(&m.FKField, name)). has_one and has_many create no FK constraint themselves; the belongs_to on the other side does. Many-to-many join tables get a composite primary key plus two FKs with ON DELETE CASCADE.

Generator diagnostics (nothing is written for the package until fixed): more than one relation kind on a field; field type does not match the kind; target is not a Momo model; fk missing or naming a missing field; many2many without join:, or a declared reverse side without join:; polytype without polyvalue (or the reverse), or on a kind other than has_one/has_many; polytype column not a field of the target; many-to-many to the model's own type; momo.Model embedded by pointer; a generic model; size on a non-string; dim on a non-vector; sparsevec or bit field without dim; scale without precision; notnull on a pointer; nullable primary key; unknown tag option; Go type with no SQL mapping.

What the generator emits per model Task (package task):

  • task.Table (a momo.TableRef), one column variable per field (task.ID, task.Title), task.As("t") for aliased columns, task.ColumnByName(name) and task.ColumnNames() (an allowlist for user-supplied sort/filter names).
  • One momo.Relation[Parent, Child] per relation field (document.Comments, document.Author).
  • Vector fields become momo.VectorColumn[vector.Vector] (nullable: NullVectorColumn).
  • read_only / create_only / immutable fields become permission-typed columns that have no Set (or insert-only Set).
  • Package name = lowercase model name. It can collide with your local variable names (task := ... shadows the package). Name variables differently or alias the import.

docs.title: Client-generated ids
docs.text:
Databases that keep ids as text and generate them in the client (Prisma @default(cuid())) have no column default to lean on. Declare the generator on the field, with the tag or in MomoConfig:

package main

import "github.com/azrtydxb/momo"

func main() {}

type Contact struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:contacts"`
    ID         string `momo:"pk,idgen:cuid"`
    Name       string
}

type Note struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:notes"`
    ID         string `momo:"pk"`
}

func (n *Note) MomoConfig(c *momo.Config) { c.IDGen(&n.ID, "ulid") }
  • Built-in generators: cuid (25 characters in the layout Prisma writes, so old and new ids look alike), uuid (random, version 4, 36 characters) and ulid (26 characters, sortable by creation time). Register your own, or replace a built-in, with momo.New(drv, momo.WithIDGenerator("short", fn)) and tag idgen:short. Names are lowercase; the MomoConfig form takes a string literal.
  • The generator fires when an insert writes the field and it holds the Go zero value: Model, Models, Upsert and every chunk of a bulk insert. An id you assigned is kept. The generated id is stored in your struct (the model you passed, or the slice element), so read m.ID after Exec or Rows.
  • The field must be a string kind (named string types and *string work). Any other type, a name given twice (tag and MomoConfig) or identity/serial on the same field is refused by the generator. A name that is neither built in nor registered fails the insert with ErrValidation.
  • A column named in Omit always takes a fresh generated id, which is bound and written back like any other. InsertQuery.Values and InsertQuery.ValuesRows that leave the id out get one too. SQL() shows a generated id in the arguments but does not store it in the model.
  • On an OnConflict upsert whose target is not the primary key, the row in the database may keep its own id. Exec then asks the database for the stored id and writes that into the model (a DoUpdate that hit an existing row gives that row's id). A model whose row DoNothing skipped keeps the id it had, usually empty. This needs RETURNING; without it (MySQL) the id is not written back for such statements. Rows never writes back there: read the id from the returned rows.
  • When the id is written back up front (every statement except the conflict case above), it stays in your struct also when the insert fails. Retrying the same struct reuses the id, and so do all rows of a failed chunked insert. Clear the field to get a new one. In the conflict case the model is updated only after a successful statement.
  • In the conflict case, rows are matched to models on the conflict-target columns (or on the generated id for DoNothing without a target), so those columns must read back exactly as you wrote them; citext, char(n) and numeric columns may not. A returned row that matches no model fails with ErrValidation and the write is rolled back; only a pinned OnConn handle, which cannot open a transaction, keeps it. If two models share a target value, the first one is matched. A non-primary-key generated column (such as a public_id) counts as a conflict case too, because the kept row has its own; the default DO UPDATE set of Upsert leaves such a column out, so a conflict never replaces the stored value, even one you assigned; to overwrite it, pass an explicit DoUpdate that sets it. A single-statement insert that reads ids back runs in its own transaction (or savepoint), so a mismatch rolls the write back, and the models are updated only after the whole insert has committed. Inside your own Tx that means after the savepoint is released, not after your outer commit: if you roll the outer transaction back, the models still hold the ids of rows that no longer exist.
  • The generator is a client-side convenience, not a secret. A cuid is built from the time, a counter and a process fingerprint, so it is guessable: do not use it for tokens or anything that must be unpredictable. Use uuid (random, version 4) or your own generator for that.
  • A generator that returns an empty id, panics, or is registered with a nil function fails the insert with ErrValidation. The ulid generator does the same in the unlikely case that it runs out of ids within one millisecond.
  • The tag adds no database default: the column stays text primary key.

docs.title: Database defaults
docs.text:
InsertQuery.Model writes every writable column, so a column with DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() or DEFAULT now() is overwritten by the Go zero value. Tag the field dbdefault to leave it to the database instead:

package main

import (
    "time"

    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
)

func main() {}

type Event struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:events"`
    ID         string    `momo:"pk,type:uuid,default:gen_random_uuid(),dbdefault"`
    Title      string
    OccurredAt time.Time `momo:"default:now(),dbdefault"`
}
  • When the field holds its zero value (the Go zero value, a nil pointer, or a value whose IsZero method reports true, such as time.Time{}), Model and Models leave the column out of the INSERT, so the database default applies, and Exec reads the stored value back with RETURNING into the struct you passed (the slice element for Models) once the statement has committed. A non-zero value is written as given. A pointer to a zero value counts as set.
  • Models with a mix of zero and set rows writes DEFAULT for the zero rows (PostgreSQL). SQLite cannot put DEFAULT in a multi-row VALUES list, and Unnest and Copy have no per-row default, so they fail with ErrUnsupported for such a mix: insert the rows separately or give every row a value. A column that is zero in every row simply leaves the column list. Copy has no RETURNING to read the value back, so it refuses a zero dbdefault column with ErrUnsupported: set a value, or use Models.
  • MySQL has no RETURNING, so a zero dbdefault column fails with ErrUnsupported there instead of leaving the struct stale: set the value, or leave it out with Omit and read it yourself. MariaDB and SQLite read it back with RETURNING.
  • Your own Returning list turns the automatic read-back off; Rows returns the columns you named. A single Model that a conflict action skips (DoNothing) returns no row: Exec reports 0 rows affected and leaves the model as it was. A bulk Models insert that returns fewer rows than models (a conflict action, a trigger or a rule dropped some) is matched by key when it can be: the key is the conflict target, else the primary key, it must be written from the model (not omitted, identity or read-only) and must not be a dbdefault column that is zero in some row. The key is then added to the RETURNING list, the returned rows are written back by key and the other models stay untouched; the insert fails only when the conflict action is DoNothing and a skipped model still has a dbdefault column unread. When the rows cannot be matched by key the insert fails with ErrUnsupported ("returned N rows for M models"), rolls back and writes nothing back: give the columns a value, or use Returning and Rows. Inside a caller's Tx the rollback is to a savepoint, not the caller's transaction, which stays open. A pinned OnConn handle cannot roll back: it returns the same error, says the returned rows were stored, and writes nothing back. The conflict-target column of an insert that also uses an id generator cannot be a dbdefault column that is zero in some row (ErrValidation). The default DO UPDATE set of Upsert leaves a dbdefault column out when a row leaves it to the database, so a conflict keeps the stored value.
  • The zero value means "use the default". On a bool or numeric column that means false and 0 can never be written explicitly through Model: a dbdefault field with DEFAULT true always stores true when it is false in Go. Write such a value with InsertQuery.Values, or do not tag the column. The same holds for an empty string and a zero time. A pointer or nullable field is refused by the generator, because nil would stop meaning NULL; write NULL with InsertQuery.Values and SetNull. Omit still wins: an omitted column is not written, and a Go-side default hook still fills it.
  • dbdefault cannot be combined with identity, serial, idgen, read_only, version, soft_delete, created_at or updated_at; the generator reports it. It adds no database default (use default:), and momo generate --from-db writes it for NOT NULL PostgreSQL columns whose default is computed (a function call, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, or a nextval sequence on a column that is not identity or serial); with introspect.dbdefault: all it writes it for every NOT NULL column that has a default, a constant one such as DEFAULT 1 included. A hand-written model can put dbdefault on any NOT NULL column that has a database default. It never writes it for other dialects: plain MySQL cannot read the value back.

docs.title: Model hooks
docs.text: Give a model a method named BeforeInsert, BeforeUpdate, BeforeDelete or AfterLoad with the exact signature func(context.Context) error and momo generate wires it into Meta.Hooks; nothing else to register. A method with a hook name and another signature fails the generator with a positioned diagnostic, and a hook-named method on a projection is a diagnostic too (projections run no hooks). The semantics (which builders run which hook, the copy BeforeInsert receives, the error kind) are in the HookSet documentation. DON'T edit Meta.Hooks in generated code.

docs.title: View models
docs.text:
A model that maps a database view embeds momo.View next to momo.Model:

type ActiveUser struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:active_users"`
    momo.View
    ID int64 `momo:"pk"`
}

The generator sets Meta.View. Reads work as for any model; Insert, Upsert, Update, SoftDelete, BulkUpdate, Delete and Merge return ErrValidation naming the model, at run time (there is no compile-time check). Declare the view itself with c.View(schema.View{...}) in MomoConfig. The schema the generator builds holds that view and no table for the view model, so a migration never issues CREATE TABLE for it, and no foreign key refers to it. Materialized: true declares a materialized view; refresh it with momo.RefreshMaterializedView(ctx, db, "name", false) (a name with a schema prefix, two parts joined by a dot, is split and quoted; the last argument adds CONCURRENTLY, which needs a unique index in the view's Indexes). It is PostgreSQL only and returns ErrUnsupported elsewhere.

docs.title: Generated servers
docs.text: The momo binary has built-in graphql, grpc and openapi plugins, enabled in the plugins section of momo.yaml. They generate servers over your models with no authentication or authorization: wrap them. The openapi and grpc plugins take ops, read_only and on_error; the OpenAPI document has a <Model> output schema and a <Model>Input request schema. See capabilities for the options, error mapping and limits.

docs.title: Custom generator binary
docs.text: The momo binary runs no custom plugins. To run your own gen.Plugin, write a main that calls cli.Main(plugins...) from github.com/azrtydxb/momo/cli and build it; it behaves as momo does and the plugins are enabled by name in the plugins section of momo.yaml.

docs.title: Projections
docs.text:
A projection reads a column subset or aggregate into a non-table struct. Embed momo.Projection by value; momo generate emits its MomoMeta into momo_gen.go (every exported field, in declaration order; column name from the naming rule or a momo:"column:..." tag). NEVER hand-write MomoMeta for a projection. The Columns(...) list of the query must equal the struct field order.

type Card struct {
    momo.Projection
    ID    int64
    Title string
    Score int64
}

Use it like this:

cards := momo.Select[models.Card](q).From(article.Table).
    Columns(article.ID, article.Title, article.Score).
    OrderBy(article.ID.Asc()).
    All(ctx)

When From is a plain generated table (article.Table) with a soft-delete column (timestamp, unix or bool), the live-row filter is added automatically, exactly as for a model; WithDeleted() and OnlyDeleted() work too. Do NOT add Where(<table>.DeletedAt.IsNull()) yourself. A Join does not change this: the From table is filtered and joined tables are not. To alias use article.Table.As("a"), which keeps the filter. The filter is NOT added when From is a subquery or CTE, or a hand-built momo.TableRef{Name:..., Alias:...} (it has no soft-delete column): filter those yourself.

If a package still has a hand-written projection MomoMeta from before the generator emitted it, delete it (method and Meta variable); the generated one redeclares it.

A projection cannot be inserted, updated or deleted (it embeds Projection, not Model). Computed columns (a distance, momo.CountAll()) are valid entries in Columns. The select list is positional and not aliased: the name you give a computed column in Columns of the meta (for example distance) is only a label.

Tuple rows: for an aggregate, join or few-column read use momo.Row1 to momo.Row10 instead of declaring a projection (no struct, no generated meta). Columns is scanned positionally into the fields C1 to Cn:

counts, err := momo.Select[momo.Row2[string, int64]](q).From(article.Table).
    Columns(article.Title, momo.CountAll()).GroupBy(article.Title).All(ctx)
// counts[i].C1 is the title, counts[i].C2 the count

// SUM is NULL over no rows: a pointer type parameter reads it as nil
total, err := momo.Select[momo.Row1[*int64]](q).From(article.Table).
    Columns(momo.Sum(article.Score)).One(ctx)
// total.C1 is nil when no article matches

A Columns count different from the arity is ErrValidation (no statement is sent). Tuple rows are read-only projections: the same soft-delete rule as above applies to the From table, and After needs a unique key in OrderBy. NEVER hand-write a projection Meta for a tuple shape.

Examples: projection-pagination, vector-search (Hit).

Details: TYPE_MAPPING.md, relations.md section 1. Example: relations.

docs.title: 5. Migrations workflow
docs.text:
Flow: edit models, momo generate, momo migrate diff <name>, REVIEW the SQL, commit, momo migrate apply.

momo generate
momo migrate diff add_plan              # offline; writes 3 files into migrations/
momo migrate diff init                  # first run on an empty dir: the initial schema
momo migrate plan                       # list pending (needs DB)
export DATABASE_URL='postgres://user:pass@host:5432/app?sslmode=verify-full'
momo migrate apply                      # [--to N] [--lock-wait 30s]
momo migrate status                     # applied | pending | dirty | mismatch | missing
momo migrate drift                      # live DB vs latest applied snapshot
  • diff writes <version>_<name>.up.sql, <version>_<name>.snapshot.json and rewrites momo.sum. Commit all three. diff never overwrites; the name must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$; the version is a 14-digit UTC timestamp.
  • diff compares models with the latest snapshot, never with the database. Prints no changes and writes nothing when equal.
  • Never edit an applied migration file, even cosmetically: apply refuses on the changed checksum. For a cosmetic edit you accept: momo migrate hash, then momo migrate rehash --version V --accept (without --accept it only shows the two checksums); see migrations.md section 4. Prefer a new migration.
  • Renames are never guessed: a rename looks like drop plus add and is refused. Say it explicitly: --rename-column table.old=new, --rename-table old=new.
  • Destructive changes (drop_table, drop_column, drop_enum, a column type change) are refused without --allow-destructive. Type changes rewrite the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and fail on rows that do not cast.
  • A NOT NULL column without a default on a table that exists in the snapshot is refused (migrate.ErrStagedRequired). Give it a default:, or stage it: diff --stage, apply, backfill, check SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE c IS NULL is 0, then diff --enforce-not-null. The flag enforces every nullable column the model has as NOT NULL, not only staged ones; with NULLs left, apply fails (exit 3) and rolls back cleanly (not dirty): backfill and apply again.
  • URL: --url (warns: visible in the process list; --url - reads stdin), else migrate.url_env.postgres, else MOMO_DATABASE_URL. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 findings, 2 usage/config, 3 database/lock/execution error. An invalid migration name (diff Bad-Name) exits 3, not 2.
  • Hand-written SQL migration: momo migrate new --custom <name> writes the up file (no -- momo:generated line), a snapshot copied from the latest one and the extended momo.sum; write the SQL, then momo migrate hash and momo migrate validate. The snapshot schema must equal its parent's. Directives (first lines): -- momo:no-transaction, -- momo:split, -- momo:destructive (informational). Unknown -- momo: directive is an error.
  • Existing database: write models, momo migrate diff init (do not apply), then momo migrate baseline --version <init version>; the live schema must match the snapshot (extra objects: add globs to migrate.exclude). Example: adopt-existing-schema.
  • The first migration with a vector column runs CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "vector". pgvector must be installed on the server (image pgvector/pgvector), and the migration role must be allowed to create extensions, otherwise apply exits 3 naming the extension. An extension a superuser installs by hand goes in migrate.external_extensions in momo.yaml: no migration emits it and drift ignores it.

CI (every change):

go install github.com/azrtydxb/momo/cmd/momo@v0.6.0
momo generate --check                                   # generated code is current
momo migrate validate                                   # files vs momo.sum, version chain, forks, snapshots
momo migrate diff ci_probe | grep -qx 'no changes'      # models have a migration

The last line is derived from the code, not covered by a test: when models changed, diff writes files (exit 0) and grep fails the job; discard the files (git checkout -- migrations && git clean -fd migrations). There is no diff --check. validate already verifies momo.sum; do not run momo migrate hash in CI.

Production checklist:

  1. momo migrate validate and momo migrate plan before apply; read the SQL.
  2. One apply job per deploy, over a DIRECT connection (not PgBouncer in transaction mode: the lock is a session advisory lock).
  3. Migrate first, then roll out code; every migration must be backward compatible with the running code (add, backfill, switch, drop later; a rename is add, copy, switch, drop).
  4. Back up before any destructive, type-change or no-transaction migration.
  5. Use a migration role without statement_timeout; migrate.lock_timeout defaults to 5 s and fails fast on a blocked DDL (safe to retry).
  6. After: momo migrate status (exit 0) and momo migrate drift.
  7. Failed transactional migration: nothing persists; fix and re-run. Failed no-transaction migration leaves partial state and a dirty row: finish or undo by hand in psql, then momo migrate resolve --version V --applied or --rolled-back. Full procedure: migrations.md section 4.

Known issues, as rules (each is a filed bug):

  • For large tables declare Concurrently() on the index in MomoConfig: diff writes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own -- momo:no-transaction migration (a trailing <name>_no_tx file when the diff also has other DDL). Without it the index is a plain CREATE INDEX that blocks writes. A failed concurrent build leaves an INVALID index: drift reports it; drop it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS, then resolve --rolled-back and re-apply.
