Lock. A row in momo_migration_lock (id = 1, holder, acquired_at), created on first use. A second holder gets ErrLocked with held by pid=N host=H at=T; apply polls it like the PostgreSQL lock until --lock-wait. Unlock deletes the row only while it still carries this holder's text. A process that dies leaves the row behind: after checking that nothing is migrating, call sqlite.ForceUnlock(ctx, conn), which returns the holder it removed (there is no CLI flag). The lock and statement timeouts of the session options do nothing on SQLite; busy handling is the driver's busy_timeout.

Other differences. DDL is transactional, so one migration is one transaction. AutoMigrate skips any change to an existing table that needs a rebuild (an enum column, say) with the reason "requires a table rebuild; use a migration", because a rebuild writes the whole desired table and would also apply the changes AutoMigrate leaves alone (TestSQLiteAutoMigrateSkipsRebuilds). Index parts carry no collation in the schema, so a collation on an index key is not compared. Collation on a column is.

docs.title: 4. Failure and recovery
docs.text: Check state with momo migrate status (exit 1 when anything is dirty, mismatched or missing). Read error, shown after the colon.

docs.title: Transactional migration fails (TestPostgresApplyRecovery)
docs.text: DDL and the history row roll back; nothing the file did persists. A rolled_back row records the error. That is not dirty: status shows pending <v> <name>: <error>, and the next apply retries from statement 1. Fix the cause (or fix the file, section "editing", then momo migrate hash) and run apply again. Data-exception errors (SQLSTATE class 22) store only the code, not the message, because the message may quote data.

docs.title: Interrupted (Ctrl-C, killed, lost connection)
docs.text:
• Transactional: the server aborts the transaction; no running row survives. Same as above. After a Ctrl-C, rollback and the failure row are still written (5 s bound).
  • No-transaction: the running row was committed, so the version stays dirty (running or failed). The lock is released when the connection dies.

docs.title: No-transaction migration fails (partial state)
docs.text:
Statements before the failing one are committed. The row is failed, with statements_applied = n and the error. Every later apply stops with ErrDirty (TestApplyRefusesDirtyAndReleasesLock) until you resolve it.

  1. momo migrate status, note the version and statements_applied.
  2. Inspect the database. Statement n+1 is the one that failed.
  3. Make the database match one of two states by hand with psql:
  4. finish the file yourself, then momo migrate resolve --version V --applied (the row becomes applied, error cleared, checksum of the file as it was when the run started is kept); or
  5. undo the committed statements, then momo migrate resolve --version V --rolled-back (the row is deleted; the version is pending again and will run from statement 1). A file may be edited before the next apply: the version has no applied row, so edit, momo migrate hash, apply.
  6. resolve takes the migration lock and errors when the version has no running or failed row.

docs.title: A down migration fails (Engine.Rollback)
docs.text:
A transactional down that fails rolls back with its history update: the schema is unchanged and the row stays applied, so the database is not dirty (TestRollbackTransactionalFailureLeavesRowApplied). Fix the down and run Rollback again; if you edit the file, run momo migrate hash first.

A down with -- momo:no-transaction commits statement by statement. When one fails the row becomes failed with statements_applied = n and an error that starts with down:, and every later apply or Rollback stops with ErrDirty (TestRollbackNoTxFailureLeavesRowFailed). Both resolve states are valid; choose by what the database looks like after you repair it:

  • resolve applied (ResolveApplied): the migration is still in effect. Use it when the failed down changed nothing that matters or you undid its partial work. The row becomes applied, the error is cleared, and the version can be rolled back again (TestResolveAppliedAfterFailedDown).
  • resolve rolled_back (ResolveRolledBack): the migration is gone. Use it when you finished the down by hand. The row is deleted, the version is pending, and the next apply runs the up file again (TestResolveRolledBackAfterFailedDown).

Rollback verifies momo.sum first, down files included: an edited or added .down.sql is refused with ErrChecksumMismatch naming the file even when the matching up file is no longer in the directory (TestRollbackChecksumMismatch). It takes the migration lock like apply (TestRollbackTakesTheLock).

docs.title: Invalid index after a failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
docs.text:
PostgreSQL leaves the index in place, marked invalid, when the build fails (for example a uniqueness violation or a cancelled build). Momo does not use IF NOT EXISTS, so re-running fails with "already exists" until you drop it.

  1. momo migrate drift shows changed: index <table>.<name>: invalid index (failed CONCURRENTLY build).
  2. DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS <schema>.<name>; in psql.
  3. Fix the data or definition.
  4. momo migrate resolve --version V --rolled-back (if the row is failed), then momo migrate apply. If the failing file contained other statements, handle them per the previous subsection first.

baseline also counts an invalid index as a mismatch.

docs.title: Editing an already-applied migration
docs.text:
apply and status refuse (checksum mismatch, naming the file; status shows mismatch). momo migrate hash does not fix this. It rewrites momo.sum, but the history row still holds the old checksum, so apply still refuses. Options:

  • Revert the file (git checkout -- <file>), then write a new migration for the change. This is the supported path.
  • If the edit is cosmetic (whitespace or a comment) and you accept it: run momo migrate hash (momo.sum), then momo migrate rehash --version V to see the recorded and the new checksum, then momo migrate rehash --version V --accept to store it. Without --accept nothing changes and the command exits 1 and says so. With it, only the row of version V is updated, and the row's error column records checksum accepted by rehash at <time>: <old> -> <new>, which status shows. The edit is accepted, not run: the database is not changed, so rehash only edits that do not alter what the migration did (TestRehash, TestRehashOnPostgres, TestMigrateRehashAcceptsEditedMigration).

Editing a migration that is not applied yet (status pending) is fine: run momo migrate hash to accept it. hash records whatever is on disk, so review the printed changed:/added:/removed: list first.

A history row whose file is gone shows missing and exit 1 on status.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text: apply with nothing pending prints no pending migrations, exits 0, and runs no migration. It takes the lock (an advisory lock, not a write) but writes nothing: it does not create the history table or its meta row, so it works with a read-mostly role. When something is pending, the history table is created first (TestApplyNothingPendingWritesNothing, TestApplyNothingPendingCreatesNoHistoryTable). Running it twice, or two processes at once, is safe: the second waits for the lock, then finds nothing to do (TestConcurrentApply, TestConcurrentApplyWaits). plan, status, drift are read-only.

docs.title: 5. Production safety checklist
docs.text: What Momo enforces, what it only hints at, what it does not see. A complete worked upgrade (add column, index, rename) is examples/upgrade-database.

docs.title: Refused unless you opt in (diff, exit 1)
docs.text:
--allow-destructive is required for: drop_table, drop_column, drop_enum, and a column type change (alter_column with a different type). The file then carries -- momo:destructive. Review these. Type changes render as ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING col::type: a full table rewrite under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which fails on rows that do not cast.

Not destructive, but reported as risky: hints by diff on PostgreSQL (no flag needed): dropping an index, primary key, unique, check or foreign key; adding a unique or check constraint (both can fail on existing data).

  • ADD CHECK is written NOT VALID; its VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (a full scan that does not block writes) goes in the trailing no-transaction migration. If the validation fails, the trailing migration is failed and apply stops with ErrDirty. The constraint stays NOT VALID: it still checks new rows. Recovery: fix the offending rows, run ALTER TABLE t VALIDATE CONSTRAINT c; in psql, then momo migrate resolve --version V --applied (V is the _no_tx version). resolve --version V --rolled-back runs the whole file again from its first statement, so it is safe only when the file holds just the failed VALIDATE. If earlier statements of the file (a CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, another VALIDATE) already committed, they would fail with "already exists": use --applied after finishing by hand, or undo those statements first (see "No-transaction migration fails").
  • ADD UNIQUE on an existing table is CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY followed by ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX, both in the trailing no-transaction migration. On duplicate rows the build fails and leaves an INVALID index (drift reports it): drop it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS, fix the data, then resolve --rolled-back and re-apply (the unique index is the first statement of its file; if other statements of that file already committed, undo them first).
  • On a partitioned table (including a sub-partitioned one) ADD UNIQUE is a plain, transactional ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE, and an index declared with Concurrently() is created and dropped without CONCURRENTLY, because PostgreSQL rejects CONCURRENTLY there. ADD CHECK keeps the NOT VALID form (TestPartitionedTableConstraintsAndIndexes).
  • diff leaves out the explicit drop of an index, unique, foreign key or primary key that lists a column dropped in the same diff: DROP COLUMN removes it, and an explicit drop after it would fail. A check or an index expression or WHERE that merely mentions a dropped column's name anywhere in its text cannot be classified reliably, so its drop is written DROP ... IF EXISTS, which is correct whether or not the column took it.
  • Limit: an inline foreign key in a new CREATE TABLE cannot reference a unique constraint that the same diff adds to another table, because that unique is created in the later no-transaction migration and the foreign key would fail. Workaround: run diff twice, first the unique on the existing table, then the new table with its foreign key.
  • Not flagged at all: dropping a view, function, trigger or policy, and any change you write by hand.

The -- momo:destructive header is informational. diff writes it and --allow-destructive is the only guard, and that guard exists in diff only: apply does not read the header or scan statements, so a hand-written file with a DROP applies without confirmation. Review every .up.sql in code review.

docs.title: NOT NULL columns
docs.text:
An added NOT NULL column (or an existing column made NOT NULL) with no default, identity or generation expression is refused (ErrStagedRequired) for any table that already exists in the snapshot. diff never queries the database, so it cannot tell whether the table has rows: an empty existing table is refused too. A column that looks like a rename (same table and type as a dropped column) is refused the same way; the message names --rename-column. With --stage, then --enforce-not-null:

  1. diff --stage adds the column as nullable and prints the hint staged: T.C was added as nullable; backfill it, then run migrate diff with --enforce-not-null to emit ALTER TABLE T ALTER COLUMN C SET NOT NULL. The new snapshot records the column as nullable, like the database will have it, so validate and status agree after you apply.
  2. Apply, backfill in batches outside the migration.
  3. Check the backfill: SELECT count(*) FROM T WHERE C IS NULL must return 0.
  4. diff <name> --enforce-not-null emits ALTER TABLE T ALTER COLUMN C SET NOT NULL and records NOT NULL in the snapshot. A plain diff (without the flag) is still refused, because only you know the backfill is done. Apply it. The statement scans the table under a lock; do it when the table is quiet or add a validated CHECK first by hand.

Several columns can be staged in separate migrations before any backfill: each stays recorded as nullable until enforced, and one --enforce-not-null emits SET NOT NULL for all of them. The flag enforces every column that is nullable in the snapshot and NOT NULL without a default in the model, not only staged ones, so backfill all of them first. New NOT NULL columns stay refused.

If NULLs remain, apply of the SET NOT NULL migration fails (exit 3). The migration is transactional, so it rolls back: the version is rolled_back (not dirty), status shows it as pending with the error, and nothing changed. Finish the backfill and run apply again. Only a hand-edited -- momo:no-transaction file can leave a dirty row; settle that with momo migrate resolve --version V --applied or --rolled-back (section 4).

The same applies to an existing column made NOT NULL: diff --stage writes nothing (the snapshot already has the column nullable; the hint is only printed when the same run writes other changes), and diff <name> --enforce-not-null emits the SET NOT NULL after the backfill. --enforce-not-null only affects existing columns: a new NOT NULL column without a default still needs --stage.

A NOT NULL column with a default is not staged. A constant default is cheap on PostgreSQL 11 and later. A volatile default (random(), clock_timestamp(), gen_random_uuid(), nextval(...) and a few more well-known functions) rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; diff prints a risk: hint (PostgreSQL only) for an ADD COLUMN with one on an existing table. It only knows the built-in names it lists; a function you wrote yourself is not checked.

docs.title: Lint (momo migrate lint)
docs.text:
momo migrate lint reads the migration files and reports operations that lock a table for long, rewrite it, or lose data. Each finding has a severity, the rule, the version and 1-based statement number, and a safer alternative. It needs no database: it checks every migration in the directory, or with --db only the ones the database has not applied (Engine.LintAll, Engine.Lint, LintSQL). It exits 1 when any finding is an error; warnings alone exit 0. A table the migration creates itself is empty and never reported: a rule fires only on a table of the parent snapshot (TestMigrateLint, TestMigrateLintQuietOnSafeSQL, TestMigrateLintExitCodes).

Rule Severity Fires on Alternative not-null-without-default error ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL without DEFAULT (serial and generated exempt) add nullable, backfill in a separate migration, then SET NOT NULL not-null-without-default warning ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL (the last step of the staged flow) backfill first; on a large table validate a CHECK ... NOT VALID first column-type-change error ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE add a new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop the old one blocking-index error CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a -- momo:no-transaction migration foreign-key-without-not-valid error ADD ... FOREIGN KEY or CHECK without NOT VALID add NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a separate migration enum-add-and-use error ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE 'x' and a later statement that mentions 'x' use the value in a later migration destructive-without-directive error DROP TABLE, DROP COLUMN, DROP SCHEMA, DROP TYPE, TRUNCATE add -- momo:destructive after a review sqlite-rebuild warning a statement with the SQLite rebuild hint (LintSQL callers) batch the data copy or split the table

The rules are text heuristics on the comment-free statement. The PostgreSQL rules (the first six) run for the postgres dialect only; the destructive rule runs for every dialect. A statement built inside a DO block or a function is not seen, and a keyword inside a string literal can cause a false report. SET NOT NULL is a warning, not an error, because the staged flow (below) ends with it. The plan also sketches a --db row count rule for SQLite rebuilds; momo migrate does not select SQLite, so it is not built.

docs.title: Other items
docs.text:
• Backfills: Momo has no data-migration step. Do them in a hand-written migration (section 6) or a separate job. A long backfill inside a transactional migration holds its locks until commit and can hit lock_timeout/statement_timeout.
  • Large-table indexes: declare Concurrently() on the index in MomoConfig. diff then writes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own no-transaction migration, so the build does not block writes. Without Concurrently() the index is a plain CREATE INDEX that blocks writes while it builds. Set a role without statement_timeout for the run. A hand-written alternative: examples/custom-sql-migration.
  • Lock timeout: the default 5 s lock wait fails fast instead of queuing behind a long transaction. A retry is safe for transactional migrations.
  • Deploy order: migrate first, then roll out code, with every migration backward compatible with the running code (add before use; drop only after no code reads it; rename as add, copy, switch, drop).
  • Run once: one apply job per deploy. Concurrent applies are safe but wait up to --lock-wait.
  • Backups: take a backup or snapshot before any destructive, type-change or no-transaction migration. PostgreSQL DDL rolls back only inside a transaction; no-transaction files cannot be rolled back.
  • CI: run momo generate --check, momo migrate validate, and the model-vs-migrations probe from section 1 on every change.
  • After: momo migrate status (exit 0) and momo migrate drift.
  • Roles: CREATE EXTENSION (pgvector, and any extension the models declare) needs a role allowed to create it. A missing package or privilege is reported, with exit 3, as extension "x" is not installed (install its server package and run CREATE EXTENSION as a role that may). If a superuser creates the extension by hand, list it in migrate.external_extensions so no migration emits it (section 7).

docs.title: 6. Custom SQL migrations
docs.text:
Worked example: examples/custom-sql-migration.

momo migrate new --custom <name> (offline) writes the three files for an empty hand-written migration: <version>_<name>.up.sql (comments only, no -- momo:generated), <version>_<name>.snapshot.json (a copy of the latest snapshot with the new version and that snapshot as its parent) and the extended momo.sum. The name follows the diff rule (lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter). It needs an existing snapshot to copy: run diff first (exit 2 otherwise), and it never overwrites a file (exit 1). Write the SQL in the up file, then run momo migrate hash (the file changed after momo.sum was written) and momo migrate validate.

You can also create the files yourself:

  1. Choose a version greater than the latest and a name: 20260301120000_backfill_slug.up.sql. Do not put -- momo:generated in it.
  2. Optional directives at the top, before the first statement: -- momo:no-transaction, -- momo:split, -- momo:destructive (informational, never enforced), -- momo:generated (do not use it here) and -- momo:sqlite-foreign-keys-off (SQLite only; apply turns foreign keys off around the migration, section 3a). -- momo:ddl is not a file directive: it goes before one MySQL ALTER TABLE statement (section 9). An unknown -- momo: directive is an error.
  3. Create 20260301120000_backfill_slug.snapshot.json as a copy of the previous snapshot with version set to the new version and parent set to the previous version. The schema must stay equal to the parent's, or validate reports "custom migration ... must not change the schema".
  4. momo migrate hash, momo migrate validate, then apply.

If the SQL changes the schema, change the models too and run diff afterward, which compares against the latest snapshot as written; otherwise the next diff will try to generate the same change again.

docs.title: 6a. Go migrations
docs.text:
A data step that SQL cannot express (a backfill that calls library code, the templates an application ships in Go) is a migrate.GoMigration. It is registered on the engine with migrate.WithGoMigrations and is ordered with the SQL files by version, so it runs once, under the same lock, with a history row (kind = 'go') like any other migration.

g := migrate.GoMigration{
    Version:  "20260301120000", // 14 digits, unique among the SQL files too
    Name:     "backfill_templates",
    Checksum: "v1", // optional, see below
    Up: func(ctx context.Context, tx *momo.Tx) error {
        _, err := momo.Exec(ctx, tx, `UPDATE company SET templates_ready = true`)
        return err
    },
}
engine, err := migrate.NewEngine(drv, dir, migrate.WithDialect(pg), migrate.WithGoMigrations(g))
  • Transaction. Up receives a *momo.Tx: the migration transaction that also holds the history rows. An error or a panic rolls everything back and records rolled_back (not dirty); the next apply runs it again. The function cannot commit or roll back that transaction.
  • No transaction. Set UpNoTx instead of Up for work that cannot run in a transaction (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, a long backfill committed in batches). It receives a *momo.DB bound to the migration connection (DB.OnConn; it cannot begin a transaction). An error leaves the row failed, which is dirty: apply refuses with ErrDirty until you finish the work by hand and run resolve (section 4). Make the function safe to run again, because resolve --rolled-back runs it from the start.
  • Version. A Go migration and a SQL file cannot share a version; plan, apply and status fail with an error naming the file, and NewEngine rejects two Go migrations on one version or a bad version or name.
  • Checksum. Go code cannot be hashed. The recorded checksum is a hash of the version, the name and the optional Checksum string. When it differs from the applied row, apply refuses with ErrChecksumMismatch and status shows mismatch. Bump Checksum when you change what a migration does and want an already-migrated database flagged; leave it empty to bind only version and name.
  • Snapshot. A Go migration has a snapshot file like a custom SQL migration (<version>_<name>.snapshot.json, a copy of the previous snapshot with the new version and parent set), and no up file. It must not change the schema. migrate.ValidateOffline checks that when you pass it the registered migrations after the directory, and that every registered Go migration has a snapshot; run it from a test of the application with the same migrations. momo migrate validate does not know the application's Go migrations, so it cannot check them. diff compares against the latest snapshot, a Go migration's included, and refuses while a registered Go migration has no snapshot file yet. Note for callers: ValidateOffline gained a variadic parameter, so a call without Go migrations compiles unchanged, but a function value of the old type no longer matches.
  • Forward only. A Go migration has no down step. A rollback of the group that contains one refuses it: Engine.Rollback calls migrate.RefuseGoRollback with the history rows to roll back, before any down runs, and that returns ErrGoMigrationNotReversible for the first row of kind go; fix forward with a new migration.
  • Baseline. Baseline through a version records a go row (checksum = the identity) for every registered Go migration up to it. An engine without that registration, the CLI included, refuses to baseline past a snapshot-only version with ErrGoMigrationUnregistered, because it cannot record the row.
  • Hooks and options. Without migrate.WithGoMigrationDB, Up and UpNoTx get a bare momo.New of the engine's driver: none of the application's hooks, field hooks, clock or other options. Pass the application's *momo.DB (same driver) to WithGoMigrationDB to have its options apply.
  • The CLI cannot run them, and refuses to pass them. momo migrate apply, plan and status read only the directory; a Go migration lives in the application's binary. The snapshot file marks its place: when the directory holds a snapshot with no up file, no registered Go migration and no history row, and a pending SQL migration has a later version, apply refuses with ErrGoMigrationUnregistered (exit 1) before it runs anything, telling you to run the application's Engine.Apply. Without that, the CLI would apply the later SQL and the application's engine would then fail with ErrOutOfOrder for the Go migration for good. Once the Go migration is applied, the CLI is unblocked; a database that has one in its history shows it as missing to the CLI. The check keys on the snapshot file, so a Go migration whose snapshot file is missing is invisible to the CLI: run ValidateOffline with your Go migrations in a test of the application, which reports that. The same refusal fires for an up file that was removed and left its snapshot, so when you squash old migrations remove their snapshots too. The application runs the engine itself, at start or in a small cmd/migrate of its own:
eng, err := migrate.NewEngine(drv, dir, migrate.WithDialect(pg), migrate.WithGoMigrations(g))
if err != nil { /* ... */ }
if _, err := eng.Apply(ctx, migrate.ApplyOptions{}); err != nil { /* ... */ }

Use that binary for apply, and keep the CLI for diff, hash, validate and drift.

docs.title: 7. Adopting an existing database
docs.text:
Worked example: examples/adopt-existing-schema.

momo generate --from-db reads a live PostgreSQL database and writes the models and the init snapshot, so nothing has to be written by hand first.

  1. Run momo generate --from-db DATABASE_URL. The value is a database URL, - to read the URL from standard input, or the name of an environment variable that holds it; prefer the last two, because a URL on the command line is visible in the process list. It inspects the schemas named by migrate.schemas (default: the current schema), writes one <table>_model.go per table into the model package (--out, else introspect.out, else the first local entry of packages, else ./models) and, when the migration directory has no snapshot, the init migration and snapshot. Do not apply the init migration.
  2. Run momo generate, which writes the generated code for the new models.
  3. momo migrate baseline --version <init version>. It checks the live database against that snapshot, including view, policy and trigger text, and exits 1 with differing object kinds: ... on a mismatch, then records every migration up to that version as applied with statements_applied = 0 and apply_id = baseline, without running them. --force records anyway; use it only after reviewing the mismatch. Schema objects outside the models, such as extra extensions, count as a mismatch: add them to migrate.exclude. The run prints a hint for the extensions and skipped tables it found.
  4. From then on use diff and apply.

The models carry exact table and column names (a table or column tag is written wherever the naming preset would derive another name), Go types, nullability (a pointer, or the nullable tag for slices), defaults, size, precision and scale, enums, primary keys, identity (identity or identity:always) and serial columns, single-column indexes as tags, other indexes, unique constraints, checks and comments in the MomoConfig method, every foreign key the generator can derive as a belongs_to field with its on_delete and on_update actions (with fk_name when the constraint name is not <table>_<column>_fkey; PostgreSQL picks _fkey1 on a partitioned table), and every composite (multi-column) foreign key to a modeled table as a c.ForeignKey(...) statement in MomoConfig. A composite primary key whose column order differs from the field order is declared with c.PrimaryKey(&m.Name, &m.Scope, &m.At) in MomoConfig; the DDL, inspection and baseline keep that order. Changing the order of an existing key later is a drop and add of the primary key under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and the drop is gated as destructive. numeric columns are Go strings (the decimal-as-string note); an introspect.types rule picks a decimal type instead. tsvector columns become types.TSVector (*types.TSVector when nullable); an introspect.types rule still overrides that.

momo generate leaves out type errors that come from files with momo's generated header, since it rewrites them. After you rename or remove a field, one momo generate run regenerates the stale file; an error in a hand-written file still stops it.

A column type with no Go mapping is an error and nothing is written; add a rule to the introspect section of momo.yaml. Constraints the models cannot declare are left out of the models and the snapshot and printed as warnings, so the two agree and the baseline reports them: foreign keys to a table with no model, single-column foreign keys whose name is not table, column and _fkey or that do not reference a single-column primary key, expression keys with an order or operator class, generated columns, and PostgreSQL schemas other than the current one.

docs.title: The introspect section
docs.text:
momo.yaml holds what the database cannot say, and it is applied again on every run:

introspect:
  package: models # default: the directory name
  out: ./models # default: the first local entry of packages
  skip: ["_prisma_*"] # table globs: no model, not in the snapshot
  only: [] # table globs: models only for these tables; skip applies within
  functions: "" # "all": every database function on the first model
  dbdefault: "" # "all": dbdefault on every NOT NULL column with a default
  uuid: google # uuid columns as github.com/google/uuid types, no type tag (default: momo, types.UUID)
  types: # SQL type to Go type, for every column of that type
    inet: { go: string }
    numeric(12,2):
      { go: decimal.Decimal, import: github.com/shopspring/decimal }
  columns: # first to last; later rules win, tags add up
    - match: "*.updated_at" # glob over table.column
      tags: [updated_at]
    - match: "users.settings"
      go: "types.JSON[Settings]"
      name: Prefs # Go field name
  tables:
    users: { name: Account, tags: ["soft_delete:timestamp"] }

uuid is momo (the default, types.UUID and []types.UUID) or google (uuid.UUID, *uuid.UUID and []uuid.UUID from github.com/google/uuid). Neither writes a type tag. introspect.uuid has no effect on MySQL, which has no uuid mapping. google makes the generated models import github.com/google/uuid, so your module must require it.

A rule's tags are momo tag options; one with the key of a generated option replaces it. A Go type needs no import for types., vector., time., json. or sql.. Add skipped tables to migrate.exclude too, so the baseline ignores the live tables.

only is the inverse of skip, for a project that moves onto momo one module at a time: when it is set, a table that matches none of its globs gets no model and no place in the init snapshot, and migrate (drift, baseline, diff) treats it as excluded, so no migrate.exclude entry is needed for it. A glob matches the table name or schema.name (only: ["app.*"]), as migrate.exclude does, and an empty entry is an error. skip applies within only, and a skipped table still needs its migrate.exclude entry.

only hides tables, and with them their triggers and policies. Inspection does not read a table outside only, so one the schema model cannot represent does not fail the run, and migrate diff ignores such a table in the snapshot, so it never plans DROP TABLE for it. It does not hide views, functions, enums or extensions of the modules you have not moved: drift still lists them as unmanaged and --from-db still writes the views and enums. Hide them with migrate.exclude. A foreign key from a modeled table to a table outside only is left out of the models and the snapshot with a warning, and the baseline reports it; add the target to only or accept the report.

By default the models carry only the functions that a modeled table's triggers, column defaults, generated columns, checks, index expressions and predicates or policies call (and the functions those call: their bodies and argument defaults, by a call or a 'name'::regproc or 'name(args)'::regprocedure literal), each on the model of the table that uses it, and a table's triggers and policies are on its own model. A function nothing modeled uses is not written. SQL built at run time (EXECUTE with a name put together from pieces) cannot be followed, so a function only that code reaches is not written and a fresh database built from the models lacks it. functions: all writes every function on the first model, as releases before 0.7.0 did, and is the workaround.

dbdefault: all tags every NOT NULL PostgreSQL column that has a default with dbdefault, constant defaults such as DEFAULT 1 included (by default only computed defaults are tagged), so InsertQuery.Model leaves an unset field to the database default. A nullable column is never tagged. See "Database defaults" in the AI guide.

docs.title: Running it again
docs.text:
The schema keeps changing during a port. A re-run rewrites the model files that nobody edited. Each file starts with a header that holds the hash of its body: when the body still matches, the file is regenerated freely. A file with hand edits, or one that --from-db did not write, is never replaced. A hand-edited file stays quiet while the database has not changed its model; it conflicts only when the regenerated model differs. The run writes the regenerated version next to it as <file>.new, prints conflict: <file>, and exits 1; merge the two by hand and delete the .new file, or run again with --overwrite to take the regenerated one. --overwrite only replaces a conflicting file: an edited file whose model the database did not change stays as it is. A file whose table is gone is printed as orphan and never deleted. --check writes nothing, prints stale: <file> for each difference and exits 1. The init snapshot is written once: when the migration directory already has a snapshot, use diff for later schema changes. Put code of your own in other files and rules in the introspect section, and a re-run stays quiet.

baseline needs CREATE on the database for the canonicalization step when the snapshot has views, functions, triggers or policies, or any table with text PostgreSQL rewrites: a column default or generation expression, a check constraint, an index predicate or an index expression. A snapshot of plain tables, columns, keys and plain indexes needs no such privilege (TestBaselineAsAppRole). --force does not waive it: the error is ErrCanonicalizePrivilege, naming the privilege, and nothing is recorded (TestBaselineAsAppRoleNeedsCreateForTableText). Run the baseline once as a role that has CREATE on the database (for example the owner role), or grant it for that run. It takes the lock and refuses on dirty or checksum problems like apply.

docs.title: Roles and extensions (verified)
docs.text:
Checked on CI with a role that is not a superuser and has no CREATE on the database:

  • CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector succeeds when the extension already exists (PostgreSQL only emits a notice; it checks existence before privileges). So the statement that a generated migration emits is harmless for that role once a superuser has installed pgvector (TestAppRoleExtensionIfNotExists). When the extension is not installed the statement needs a privileged role, as before.
  • baseline and apply run CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS for the history table. PostgreSQL checks CREATE on the schema before it looks for the table, so a role with only USAGE on the schema is refused with the error permission denied for schema even when it owns an existing momo_migrations (TestBaselineAsAppRoleNeedsCreateOnSchema). The migrator role needs CREATE on its schema: GRANT CREATE ON SCHEMA app TO app_role.
  • With CREATE on the schema but not on the database, baseline works for a snapshot without table text (TestBaselineAsAppRole) and fails with ErrCanonicalizePrivilege otherwise (section 7). drift fails with it when the snapshot declares a view, a trigger WHEN or a policy expression, and runs without it for table text only, listing the tables in CanonicalizeSkipped (TestDriftBodiesNeedCreateOnDatabase, TestDriftTablesOnlyRunsAsApplicationRole).

docs.title: Extensions managed outside momo
docs.text:
Set migrate.external_extensions in momo.yaml for an extension that a superuser installs by hand:

migrate:
  external_extensions: [vector]

Names are exact. For each listed extension momo

  • never emits CREATE EXTENSION from diff (or AutoMigrate), even when a model has a vector column, and keeps it out of the snapshot it writes;
  • does not report it from drift, and does not count it as a mismatch in baseline, even though the live database has it.

The migrations then no longer create the extension, so a new environment must get it before the first apply. Use it only when that is the intent. It differs from migrate.exclude, which hides unmanaged objects of every kind from drift and baseline but does not stop diff from emitting CREATE EXTENSION for a model that needs it. If a snapshot already declares the extension, the setting hides it on both sides, so no drop or create is generated either.

A database that uses serial or bigserial ids is adopted with the serial tag, as in pk,serial on an int64 field. The tag renders smallserial, serial or bigserial by the Go integer width. Inspection reads a column whose default is nextval of a sequence owned by the column back as the same serial column, so the snapshot matches and diff stays empty. serial is PostgreSQL only; other dialects refuse it. Turning an existing column into or out of serial is refused by diff, with an error that asks for a hand-written migration.

Upgrade note: inspection used to report a serial column as identity. If you adopted a serial database with pk,identity on the model, or kept a snapshot taken from one, diff now stops with column "id" is a serial column in the database but the model declares identity. Change the tag to pk,serial and regenerate the snapshot; or write a migration that converts the column to identity. Momo does not treat the two as equal, because a new environment would then be built with identity while production keeps its serial.

AutoMigrate is a Go API for development and tests. It applies additive changes only, writes no history and no files, and returns the rest as Skipped. Do not mix it with versioned migrations on one schema.

docs.title: 7a. Cutover from Prisma db push to momo
docs.text:
Playbook for a database whose schema is changed by prisma db push and hand-written idempotent SQL files (DO $$ ... IF NOT EXISTS guards, GRANT lines, a hand-created extension), moving to momo owning the DDL. Rehearse every step on a copy of production.

  1. Models first. Write the momo models so they match the live database (section 7). Columns Prisma generates in the client, such as cuid ids, are not in the database; model them as plain columns.
  2. Declare what you do not own. Put the extension a superuser installs in migrate.external_extensions. Put tables, views and functions that stay outside the models (an analytics schema, an audit table, Prisma's _prisma_migrations) in migrate.exclude. Roles, grants and sequences outside a column are not part of the schema model; they stay in hand-written SQL.
  3. Write the initial migration. momo migrate diff init against an empty directory. Do not apply it. Read the generated SQL: it is what a new environment would run, and it must build the schema you have.
  4. Rehearse the baseline on a copy, with momo migrate baseline --version <init version>, as a role with CREATE on the database (section 7). Exit 1 lists the differing object kinds. Fix the models or exclude until it is clean. Do not use --force to skip a difference you have not read.
  5. Dual-writer period: momo watches, it does not write. While Prisma still pushes, the database moves under momo. Do not baseline production yet and do not apply migrations. Run momo migrate drift against a baselined copy, or the rehearsal in step 4 against production, on a schedule. A table Prisma added shows as unmanaged:, a new column in a managed table as changed: ... not in snapshot, and an altered column as changed:. Each is a task: put it in the models, or in exclude. Drift cannot see changed view, trigger or policy text (section 1).
  6. Freeze db push. Stop prisma db push in every environment (remove it from the deploy). Update the models to the final live state and, since nothing was applied, delete the unapplied init files and run diff init again, so the initial snapshot is the schema as it is at the freeze.
  7. Baseline each environment. In each environment run momo migrate baseline --version <init version> once, then momo migrate drift (expect no drift). The role that runs apply needs CREATE on the schema (section 7). From then on apply runs only newer migrations. A database created from scratch runs the init migration; it needs the external extension installed first.
  8. Hand off. Schema changes go through diff; backfills and other data changes through momo migrate new --custom, which replaces the hand-written SQL files. Leave guards such as IF NOT EXISTS out of new files: the history says what ran.

Undo: baseline only writes history rows, so drop the momo_migrations table to return to the state before step 7; nothing else changed.

docs.title: 8. Security
docs.text:
• momo redacts connection strings from everything it prints (stdout, stderr, error text, and bad flag values that a pasted URL lands in): URL userinfo becomes ***@, a URL in text that has a query keeps the part before ? and shows ?***, a password=/passwd=/pwd= value becomes ***, and the exact URL and password given are replaced by ***. History error text is the server message only, never Detail. Messages of SQLSTATE class 22 (data exception) are withheld because they can contain data values. Connection URLs and password= values in the text are replaced by *** before it is stored (TestHistoryErrorIsRedacted).
  • A warning on stderr (not a failure) when a command that needs a database is given a URL with sslmode=disable and any non-local host: TLS is not enforced (sslmode=disable) for remote host H: credentials and data can cross the network unencrypted; use sslmode=verify-full. It names the hosts only. It also fires when the URL or key=value string has no sslmode (libpq then uses prefer, which falls back to plaintext), for allow and prefer, for key=value connection strings, and when sslmode comes from PGSSLMODE; a host missing from the string is read from PGHOST. localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, unix socket paths and no host at all do not warn, and neither do require, verify-ca and verify-full. require encrypts but does not check the server's identity, so use sslmode=verify-full against a real server.
  • Do not pass the URL with --url on shared hosts (momo warns); use migrate.url_env, MOMO_DATABASE_URL or --url - (stdin).
  • Review *.up.sql in code review like any code: apply runs it as the connected role, and momo.sum only detects change, not intent.
  • Tamper detection is against accidental edits, not an attacker. momo migrate hash rewrites momo.sum to match whatever is on disk, and momo migrate rehash --accept stores the checksum of whatever file is on disk in the history row. Both trust the files completely: anyone who can edit the migration files and run those commands can make an edited migration pass every check. Protect the migration directory with code review and write access control, and the database with the migrator role's grants; momo.sum does not.
  • drift and baseline execute model DDL on the target database. To compare declared text with what the database reports, they create a scratch schema and run the declared definitions (defaults, checks, index predicates, view queries, function bodies, policy and trigger expressions) in a transaction that is rolled back. That needs CREATE on the database, runs SQL taken from your snapshots and models, and takes locks while it runs. Run them against a scratch database restored from a backup, or a clone, rather than production.

docs.title: 9. MySQL and MariaDB
docs.text:
The migrate/mysql package is the migration dialect for MySQL 8.4, MySQL 9.7 and MariaDB 11.8. It reads information_schema, renders DDL and locks with GET_LOCK. momo migrate does not select it yet; build the engine with migrate.WithDialect(mmysql.New()) and the mysqldriver driver.

Every migration is non-transactional. DDL implies a commit on these servers, so a failure cannot be rolled back. The engine runs each statement on its own, records statements_applied after each one, and leaves a failed row that is dirty until you repair the database and run resolve. This holds with or without -- momo:no-transaction, for Go migrations, and for rollback: a down that fails half-way leaves its earlier statements applied and the row failed. Write each migration so that a half-applied run is easy to finish by hand.

Locking. GET_LOCK names are server-wide, so the lock name carries the database (momo:<database>.momo_migrations, cut to the 64 characters MySQL allows, with a hash suffix when the key is longer). The lock belongs to the pinned connection and is released with RELEASE_LOCK, or when the connection ends. A busy lock returns migrate.ErrLocked with the connection id of the holder.

Session timeouts. The lock timeout becomes lock_wait_timeout, the time a statement waits for a metadata lock, in whole seconds. A statement timeout becomes max_statement_time on MariaDB; on MySQL it is refused with momo.ErrUnsupported, because max_execution_time bounds SELECT only.

Online DDL. A line -- momo:ddl ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE directly before an ALTER TABLE statement appends those options to it. MySQL rejects LOCK=NONE together with ALGORITHM=INSTANT; use ALGORITHM=INSTANT alone. The server rejects the statement when it cannot honour them, so a change that would copy the table fails instead of running slowly. Without the directive momo adds no ALGORITHM or LOCK clause. Only ALGORITHM= and LOCK= options are accepted.

What inspection reports. One database is inspected, the connection's default, and the history table is left out.

  • A UNIQUE constraint and a unique index are the same object on these servers. A unique key made of plain ascending columns is reported as a unique constraint; declare such keys as constraints.
  • The index MySQL creates for a foreign key, named after the constraint, is not reported, and the diff refuses a declared index that has the name of a foreign key of its table, because the two would collide and could not be told apart. An index of a database you adopt that already has such a name and the key's columns is treated as the server's own.
  • NO ACTION is reported as an empty action. MariaDB reports its default as RESTRICT, so on MariaDB RESTRICT and an unwritten clause are one.
  • MariaDB stores json as longtext with a json_valid check named after the column; the pair is reported as type json.
  • A column is reported with a collation only when it differs from its table's default; declare Collate on the column to pin one.
  • Defaults that the servers store alike are one default: NOW, LOCALTIME and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP; TRUE and FALSE are 1 and 0. RESTRICT and NO ACTION are the same foreign key action.
  • Stored CHECK text is compared without the identifier quotes, character set introducers and the parentheses MySQL adds around each comparison. Other rewrites by the server (for example != stored as <>) show as a difference of text; write the expression the way the server stores it. Parentheses around a comparison are removed only between and, or and xor, so (a between 1 and 2) and c > 0 keeps them and differs from the same text without them; a backslash escape inside a string is kept as written.
  • A foreign key into another database is reported as database.table.
  • Integer display widths (int(11) on MariaDB) are no difference of type. Identifier quotes, character set introducers and outer parentheses in stored expressions are no difference of text.
  • An index part with a prefix length is the column name followed by the length in parentheses, such as name(10). Index visibility, character sets and ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are not part of the schema model, and a MODIFY COLUMN that a type change renders restates the column without them: an ALTER of such a column is a migration to write by hand.

Rendering. Tables are ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4. An identity column is AUTO_INCREMENT (by_default; always and serial are refused). A default that is not a literal or CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is wrapped in parentheses, as MySQL requires. Partial indexes, storage parameters, operator classes, enums, views, functions, triggers and policies have no MySQL rendering yet and are refused. The hash index method is refused: InnoDB builds it as BTREE. Dropping a foreign key also drops the index MySQL built for it, when one exists, unless another foreign key of the table starts with the same column: that key may rely on the index, and dropping it would fail after the key was gone. The index then stays and shows as an index named like the dropped key; declare it, or drop it once nothing needs it. An AUTO_INCREMENT column must be a key in the statement that adds it, but the engine adds a primary key in a separate statement after the column: add such a column and its key in a migration you write yourself. Declare a generated column as nullable: MariaDB does not take NOT NULL on one. MySQL refuses a CHECK, or a stored generated column, on a column that a foreign key with a referential action uses.

docs.title: Upgrading: generated file header
docs.text:
Generated Go files start with // Code generated by momo (format 1). DO NOT EDIT.. The header carries the generated-file format number, which decides compatibility, and no momo release version, so a later momo upgrade does not rewrite generated files whose code is unchanged. Earlier releases wrote the same line with a release version between momo and (format 1); momo still recognises that form, so orphan detection keeps working.

After upgrading, run momo generate once. Until then momo generate --check reports the header change in every generated file.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text: None open. Fixed issues are listed in the changelog.

docs.title: momovet: static check for raw SQL
docs.text: Momo binds every value as a parameter, but the raw-SQL functions take the statement text as a Go string. A string built with + or a format call from user input is an injection point. The momovet analyzer reports it.

docs.title: What it reports
docs.text:
A call to one of these functions of github.com/azrtydxb/momo whose SQL argument is not a constant:

Function SQL argument momo.Exec third (after the context and the querier) momo.Scalars third (after the context and the querier) momo.MapRows third (after the context and the querier) momo.Query third (after the context and the querier) momo.QueryRows third (after the context and the querier) momo.RawQuery second (after the querier) momo.SQL first momo.TypedSQL first momo.RawSubquery first

A constant is a string literal, a const, or an expression made only of constants ("UPDATE t SET " + "x = 1"). Anything else is reported as non-constant SQL string passed to momo.<Name>. Pass values as arguments after the SQL text instead of concatenating them.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
go install github.com/azrtydxb/momo/cmd/momovet@latest
go vet -vettool="$(which momovet)" ./...

It also runs standalone: momovet ./....

To embed it in your own multichecker, import github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momovet and use its Analyzer variable.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The analyzer does not follow assignments. A var that holds a literal is reported, even a package-level one that is never reassigned: this is a false positive by design, so declare it as a const. It checks the call site only, so SQL built in one function and passed through another is reported where it reaches a raw-SQL function.

docs.title: MySQL and MariaDB
docs.text: What works on MySQL and MariaDB today, and what does not. The driver is driver/mysqldriver (database/sql on github.com/go-sql-driver/mysql). The migration dialect migrate/mysql exists as a library; the momo migrate command does not run it (see Migrations and the generated status in capabilities).

docs.title: Supported servers
docs.text:
Server Version Image used in CI MySQL 8.4 LTS 8.4.13 mysql:8.4.13 MySQL 9.7 LTS 9.7.4 mysql:9.7.4 MariaDB 11.8 LTS 11.8.9 mariadb:11.8.9

No innovation releases are supported. CI runs the shared suites against all three servers (the integration-mysql job), on every push.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Open the pool with mysqldriver.Open(dsn, flavor), or build the DSN with mysqldriver.ConfigureDSN and pass the *sql.DB to mysqldriver.New. The configured DSN always has:

  • parseTime=true and loc=UTC, and the session time_zone set to +00:00;
  • clientFoundRows=true, so an UPDATE reports the rows it matched;
  • interpolateParams=false and multiStatements=false: values always travel as bound parameters of a prepared statement and never become SQL text. A DSN that sets either is overridden. A *sql.DB handed to New directly must already be configured this way.

Open pings the server, as the SQLite drivers do, so a bad DSN, a refused connection or bad credentials fail at Open and not on the first statement. An unknown flavor makes Open return ErrUnsupported; on any error the pool is closed and nothing is returned. (New, which takes an already opened *sql.DB, still returns a driver whose every call is ErrUnsupported for an unknown flavor, because it has no error to return.)

ConfigureDSN (and so Open) refuses two DSN settings with ErrValidation:

  • allowAllFiles=true, which lets the server read any client file through LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE;
  • allowCleartextPasswords=true, which sends the password unhashed.

Remove them from the DSN. The error message never quotes the DSN.

Transport security is the DSN's business and defaults to none: add tls=true (or a registered TLS config) for any server that is not on the same host.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
The rows below are checked against dialect.MySQLFlavor by TestCapabilityMatrixMatchesDialect.

Capability mysql mariadb Returning no no InsertReturning no yes OnConflict no no OnDuplicateKey yes yes NullsOrdering no no TransactionalDDL no no Merge no no ILike no no Locking yes yes RowValues yes yes Savepoints yes yes Vector.Storage yes yes Vector.Metrics none l2, cosine Vector.Indexes none vector

Returning is the UPDATE and DELETE form. MariaDB 11.8 can return rows from an INSERT only (INSERT ... RETURNING), which is why it has InsertReturning set while Returning stays false: Returning on an insert works on MariaDB, and on an update or delete it is ErrUnsupported on both servers. MySQL has no RETURNING at all.

docs.title: Writes
docs.text:
• A single Model insert reads LAST_INSERT_ID and writes it into the identity field of the model. A key generated on the Go side (an id generator) always wins; LAST_INSERT_ID is read only for a key the database generates. A multi-row insert returns and writes back no keys, because the ids of a multi-row statement depend on innodb_autoinc_lock_mode. On MariaDB, ask for them with Returning; on MySQL that is ErrUnsupported. The LAST_INSERT_ID write-back does not apply to an upsert or to any insert with a conflict clause (wantsGeneratedKey in the core is false for them), because the statement may update an existing row and LAST_INSERT_ID then does not name the row's key; read the row back with a query.
  • Upserts render as INSERT ... VALUES ... AS momo_new ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE on MySQL and with VALUES(col) on MariaDB. DoNothing renders a no-op assignment of a key column. A Where on a conflict clause is ErrUnsupported.
  • ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE fires for a conflict on any unique key and cannot name one. Momo therefore accepts a conflict target only when it is the only unique key of the table, the primary key included; otherwise the call is ErrUnsupported. Without a schema (a hand-written model) only a primary-key target is accepted.
  • With clientFoundRows, an upsert reports 1 for an inserted row, 2 for an existing row that changed, and 1 for an existing row set to its current values. DoNothing also reports 1 for a skipped row. A count of 1 does not tell an insert from a skip.
  • A bare OFFSET gets LIMIT 18446744073709551615 in front of it, because MySQL and MariaDB reject an offset without a limit.

docs.title: Locking and transactions
docs.text: ForUpdate and ForShare render FOR UPDATE and FOR SHARE; NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED are passed through. MariaDB 11.8 has no FOR SHARE, so it gets LOCK IN SHARE MODE. LockOf (FOR UPDATE OF) is MySQL only; on MariaDB it is ErrUnsupported. Savepoints and the four standard isolation levels work; read-only transactions use START TRANSACTION READ ONLY. Any other isolation level is ErrUnsupported. ForNoKeyUpdate and ForKeyShare are PostgreSQL only and return ErrUnsupported here. timeop.ClockTimestamp renders SYSDATE(6); timeop.StatementTimestamp is ErrUnsupported.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Server errors map by number: 1062 unique, 1451 and 1452 (and 1216, 1217) foreign key, 1048 and 1364 not null, 3819 (MySQL) and 4025 (MariaDB) check, 1213 and MariaDB 1020 serialization (deadlock, and a row that changed under innodb_snapshot_isolation), 1205 and 3572 busy. Error() never shows the server text, which can quote a row value; Detail() returns it, and errors.As reaches the *mysql.MySQLError. The constraint name differs by server: MySQL 8 reports a unique key as table.index, MariaDB reports only the index name.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text: MySQL 8.4 has no vector columns. MySQL 9.7 stores VECTOR and reads it back, but offers no distance function in the Community edition (DISTANCE() is HeatWave and MySQL AI only), so every distance builder is ErrUnsupported on MySQL. MariaDB 11.8 renders vecop.L2 as VEC_DISTANCE_EUCLIDEAN and vecop.Cosine as VEC_DISTANCE_COSINE on vector.Vector columns, and its driver reports Vectors. Inner product, L1, Hamming, Jaccard and the half, sparse and bit types return ErrUnsupported on MariaDB. Details and the VECTOR INDEX rules are in vectors.md.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text: The library dialect migrate/mysql inspects information_schema, renders DDL, locks with GET_LOCK and runs every migration, up and down, statement by statement, because DDL commits implicitly on these servers. Build the engine with migrate.WithDialect and the mysqldriver driver; the inspector, drift check and -- momo:ddl online DDL options work through it. The momo migrate command still builds only the PostgreSQL dialect, so it rejects MySQL and MariaDB. What the dialect reports and renders is in migrations.md.

docs.title: Observability hooks
docs.text:
Momo calls the hooks you register with momo.WithHook around every statement (momo.Hook) and around every relation load (momo.RelationHook, for a hook that also implements it). The interfaces live in the root package because DB calls them. Ready-made implementations:

Hook Constructor What it does obs.Recorder &obs.Recorder{} (package obs) Keeps every finished statement and relation load for assertions in tests. obs.NPlusOne obs.NewNPlusOne(n, report) (obs) Reports a relation that was loaded more than n times inside one obs.WithScope. slow query obs.NewSlowQuery(d, report, opts...) Reports each statement slower than d, with an opt-in plain EXPLAIN plan. slog hook momolog.New(logger, opts...) (momolog) Logs one log/slog record per statement and one per relation load (see slog). OTel hook otelmomo.New(tp, mp, opts...) (otelmomo) Emits a client span and a duration histogram per statement (see OpenTelemetry).

obs imports only momo and the standard library. All of these hooks are safe for concurrent use.

docs.title: Arguments and sensitive columns
docs.text: A hook sees bound argument values only when the DB was opened with momo.WithArgLogging. A value bound from a column tagged sensitive reaches every hook as momo.RedactedArg ([redacted]), never as the real value, and the hooks here cannot recover it. obs.Recorder stores a copy of the arguments and hands out copies. The slog hook logs arguments only when you also pass momolog.Values(true).

docs.title: Recorder
docs.text:
rec := &obs.Recorder{}
db := momo.New(drv, momo.WithHook(rec))
// run the code under test
rec.SQLs()      // the SQL text of each statement, in order
rec.Events()    // the full momo.QueryEvent of each, plus CtxSQL
rec.Relations() // the momo.RelationEvent of each relation load, with its Err
rec.Reset()

obs.Event.CtxSQL is the value obs.Recorder put into the context in BeforeQuery; it equals SQL when the context reached AfterQuery intact, which makes it a check that the hook chain passes the context through.

docs.title: N+1 detection
docs.text:
Two detectors exist, and they count different things:

Detector Counts Scope Use it for obs.NewNPlusOne relation loads (Load, LoadAll, Preload) obs.WithScope(ctx) a relation Load inside a loop over the parents momo.NewNPlusOneHook repeated statement shapes momo.WithQueryScope(ctx) any repeated statement, such as a Select in a loop

Use either or both. Each reads only its own scope, so a context needs obs.WithScope for the first and momo.WithQueryScope for the second; a context with only one of them is not tracked by the other detector.

det := obs.NewNPlusOne(3, func(f obs.Finding) {
    log.Printf("N+1: %s loaded %d times", f.Relation, f.Count)
})
db := momo.New(drv, momo.WithHook(det))

ctx := obs.WithScope(r.Context()) // one request, one job

obs.NPlusOne counts relation loads per relation within a scope. It reports once per relation and scope, when the count first exceeds the threshold. One batched Load is one load however many parents it covers, so it never triggers a finding; a Load inside a loop over the parents does. obs.Finding.Parents is the parent count of the load that crossed the threshold; 1 is the usual sign of a loop. A context without a scope is not tracked, a scope tracks at most 1024 relations, and a panic in report is recovered and dropped. report runs on the loading goroutine and must not query the database. Create the detector with obs.NewNPlusOne; its zero value must not be used.

docs.title: Slow queries
docs.text:
obs.NewSlowQuery(threshold, report) calls report with an obs.SlowQuery (SQL, Duration, and Plan or PlanSkipped) for each statement that took longer than threshold.

plain := momo.New(drv) // a DB without the slow-query hook
db := momo.New(drv, momo.WithHook(obs.NewSlowQuery(200*time.Millisecond,
    func(q obs.SlowQuery) { log.Printf("slow %s: %s %v", q.Duration, q.SQL, q.Plan) },
    obs.WithPlainExplain(plain),
)))

Without obs.WithPlainExplain the report has no plan. With it, the hook runs one plain EXPLAIN for the slow statement, never EXPLAIN ANALYZE, so nothing runs twice. Outside a transaction the plan comes from the querier you pass; inside a transaction it runs on that transaction in a savepoint that is always rolled back, so a plan that fails cannot abort your transaction. Cases where there is no plan say why in PlanSkipped: a statement with bound arguments on a DB opened without momo.WithArgLogging, a statement that binds a sensitive value, a transaction that is already aborted (PostgreSQL), and an EXPLAIN the database rejected. The statements the hook issues for the plan are not reported again. report runs on the goroutine that ran the statement and must not query the database. The plan can echo literal values.

docs.title: Explain
docs.text: momo.Explain(ctx, q, compiled) returns the database's plan for any compiled statement (the value of a query's SQL method) without running it: EXPLAIN on PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on SQLite and EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON on MySQL and MariaDB. momo.ExplainAnalyze(ctx, q, compiled) runs the statement under EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT TEXT) and returns the plan with actual timings. It executes the statement, so every call, a SELECT included, runs inside a transaction (a savepoint on a Tx) that is always rolled back. A rollback cannot undo what happens outside the transaction: sequence values taken by nextval, NOTIFY sent by a function, work done through dblink or a foreign data wrapper. A SELECT that calls such a function still has those effects. It is PostgreSQL only: other dialects return ErrUnsupported and send nothing. Momo calls neither on its own, and hooks see both as Op explain. SelectQuery.Explain stays the shorthand for a select.

docs.title: slog
docs.text:
The slog hook is momolog.New; there is one slog hook, not two.

logger := slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stderr, nil))
db := momo.New(drv, momo.WithHook(momolog.New(logger,
    momolog.Level(slog.LevelInfo),
    momolog.SlowOver(200*time.Millisecond), // slower statements log at WARN
)))

A statement record (momo.query) has op, table, relation (when set), sql, duration, rows, err (when set) and, with momolog.Values(true) and momo.WithArgLogging, args. A relation record (momo.relation) has parent, name, kind, parents, children, queries, duration and err (when set). Errors are logged through Error() only.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
otelmomo is a separate module, github.com/azrtydxb/momo/otelmomo, so the Momo core links no OpenTelemetry package (a test runs go list -deps on the core to keep it that way). Add it to your go.mod only if you want it.

The module has its own release tags, otelmomo/vX.Y.Z, made by release-please (go get github.com/azrtydxb/momo/otelmomo@latest). It requires a released momo version (see its go.mod) whose exported API it compiles against, so it needs no unreleased momo code; the replace directive in its go.mod only points in-repository builds at the working tree and is ignored by anyone who imports it. A repository test fails if that require ever becomes a pseudo-version or names a momo version newer than the last release.

h, err := otelmomo.New(tracerProvider, meterProvider, otelmomo.WithNamespace("appdb"))
if err != nil {
    return err // a nil provider is an error; there is no global fallback
}
db := momo.New(drv, momo.WithHook(h))

The providers are passed in; the package reads no global provider. Each statement becomes a client span named <OPERATION> <table> (SELECT authors), or <OPERATION> when no table is known, with the database client attributes db.system.name (postgresql, sqlite, mysql, mariadb), db.operation.name, db.collection.name, db.namespace (from WithNamespace) and db.query.text. The query text is the parameterized SQL; the value of a bound argument is never recorded, not even with momo.WithArgLogging. A failed statement sets the span status to error and error.type. The same hook records the db.client.operation.duration histogram (unit s) with the same attributes plus error.type on failure.

docs.title: Tenants
docs.text: Tenant isolation stays row-level security through WithTxSetup; obs adds no tenant helper.

docs.title: Projections
docs.text: A projection is a result type that is not a table: a subset of a table's columns, an aggregate, or a computed column such as a vector distance. You select it with momo.Select[T], name the source with From and the select list with Columns. A projection is read only: it cannot be inserted, updated or deleted.

docs.title: Declaring one
docs.text:
Embed momo.Projection by value in a struct. Every exported field is one column of the select list, in declaration order.

type Card struct {
    momo.Projection
    ID    int64
    Title string
    Score int64 `momo:"column:points"`
}
  • The column name of a field follows the naming rule of the project (naming: in momo.yaml), as for model fields. A momo:"column:..." tag overrides it. The name is a label: the select list is positional and not aliased.
  • Unexported fields and fields tagged momo:"-" are skipped. Relation tags are an error on a projection.
  • A projection has no table, no primary key, no indexes and no MomoConfig. The generator does not add it to the schema, so it never appears in a migration.
  • A field type must be one the generator maps (see the type mapping). An unsupported type fails momo generate with a message that names the struct and the field, for example projection Odd: field Value: Go type complex128 has no SQL mapping.

docs.title: The generated metadata
docs.text: momo generate writes, for each projection, a MomoMeta method and a momo.Meta value into the momo_gen.go of the package that declares it. Columns, Ptr and Value cover every field in declaration order. Identity, Version, SoftDelete, CreatedAt and UpdatedAt are all -1, because a projection has none of those columns. Do not write this by hand. A package that holds only projections gets a momo_gen.go too.

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
cards, err := momo.Select[models.Card](q).
    From(article.Table).
    Columns(article.ID, article.Title, article.Score).
    OrderBy(article.Score.Desc(), article.ID.Asc()).
    All(ctx)

From takes the generated article.Table of a model package, an aliased table (article.Table.As("a")), a CTE or a subquery. Columns must list as many expressions as the struct has fields, in field order. Without Columns the query fails with ErrValidation. Computed expressions (a distance, momo.CountAll()) are valid entries.

Keyset pagination over a projection lists the unique tie-break key in OrderBy yourself, since the metadata has no primary key. See projection-pagination.

docs.title: Tuple rows: no struct per shape
docs.text:
For an aggregate, a join or a few columns that you read in one place, skip the struct and the generated metadata: momo.Row1 to momo.Row10 are generic projections with fields C1 to Cn. Columns is scanned positionally, so expression i fills Ci.

// a count per key
rows, err := momo.Select[momo.Row2[string, int64]](db).
    From(license.Table).
    Columns(license.Key, momo.CountAll()).
    GroupBy(license.Key).
    All(ctx)
for _, r := range rows {
    fmt.Println(r.C1, r.C2) // key, count
}

// a single aggregate
total, err := momo.Select[momo.Row1[int64]](db).From(license.Table).Columns(momo.CountAll()).One(ctx)
// total.C1
  • A column that can be NULL takes a pointer type: a LeftJoin side or an aggregate over no rows. With a Row3 of string, *int64, *string, the columns a.Title, b.ID, b.Title fill C1 to C3, and C2 and C3 stay nil when the join finds no row.
  • Subquery columns, Union, FromSubquery, SelectQuery.With and WithRecursive work as for any projection. The Go types of the columns are yours to match; they are not checked against the SQL.
  • A mismatch between the number of Columns and the arity of the row is ErrValidation, reported before any statement runs. So is omitting Columns.
  • A tuple row is a projection with no table: Insert, Update, Delete, Upsert, SoftDelete and ForceDelete refuse it with ErrValidation. It has no soft-delete column of its own, and the filter on the From table applies as described below, so a Row1[int64] with CountAll over article.Table counts live rows, and WithDeleted counts all.
  • After works when OrderBy lists a unique key, since a tuple has no primary key to break ties.
  • The metadata is built once per instantiation and shared; looking it up does not allocate.

When the result has meaning worth a name, or more than ten columns, declare a projection struct instead and let momo generate write its metadata.

docs.title: Soft-deleted rows
docs.text:
When From is the generated article.Table of a model that has a soft-delete column (timestamp, unix or bool), a projection excludes soft-deleted rows by default, exactly as a model query does. WithDeleted() includes them and OnlyDeleted() returns only them. Do not add the deleted_at predicate by hand.

The filter applies to the From table whatever else the query does: with Join or LeftJoin the From table is still filtered, and the joined tables are not (filter them in the ON clause or a Where, as for a model). To alias the table keep the generated one and call As: article.Table.As("a") keeps the soft-delete column, so the filter is qualified with the alias.

The filter is not added when:

  • From is a subquery or CTE: filter inside it;
  • From is a hand-built momo.TableRef{Name: ..., Alias: ...}: it carries no soft-delete column. Start from the generated article.Table instead, or add the predicate yourself, for example Where(article.DeletedAt.IsNull()).

docs.title: Upgrading from hand-written metadata
docs.text: Before the generator emitted projections, the guides told you to write MomoMeta and a momo.Meta value for each projection by hand. After you upgrade, momo generate writes them too, and the package no longer compiles (MomoMeta redeclared). Delete the hand-written MomoMeta method and its Meta variable for every struct that embeds momo.Projection, then run momo generate. Check that the field order and momo:"column:..." tags give the column names you had. Remove any Where(<table>.DeletedAt.IsNull()) you added to projection queries; keeping it is harmless but redundant.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

  • vector-search: Hit, a title together with its distance.
