docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
This guide covers how Momo models relations between tables: declaring them, loading them, filtering by them, writing them, and observing them. Every snippet uses the real API. The models are a small document store: Document belongs to an Author, has many Comments, and is tagged with many Tags.

Relation operations are methods and functions on the generated Relation[P, C] descriptor, where P is the parent model and C the child model. A descriptor is immutable and safe for concurrent use.

  • Declaring relations
  • Eager loading
  • Preload and single-query loading
  • Pipelined loading
  • Relation predicates and traversal
  • Association helpers
  • Graph writes
  • Observability
  • Errors and limitations

docs.title: 1. Declaring relations
docs.text:
A relation is a field on the parent model. Its tag names the kind, and the Go type of the field decides the shape:

Tag Field type Foreign key lives on belongs_to *Target the parent has_one *Target the child has_many []Target the child many2many []Target a join table 
type Author struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:authors"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    Name       string

    Documents []Document `momo:"has_many,fk:AuthorID"`
}

type Document struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:documents"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    AuthorID   *int64
    Title      string

    Author   *Author   `momo:"belongs_to,fk:AuthorID"`
    Comments []Comment `momo:"has_many,fk:DocumentID"`
    Tags     []Tag     `momo:"many2many,join:taggings"`
}

type Comment struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:comments"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    DocumentID int64
    Body       string
    Approved   bool
}

type Tag struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:tags"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    Name       string
}

The generated code lives in one package per model (author, document, comment, tag), imported next to the models package.

docs.title: Generating relation code
docs.text:
Run momo generate in the module that holds your models (or add //go:generate momo generate to a source file and run go generate ./...). It reads momo.yaml and writes the descriptors into the model packages. Commit the generated files, and use momo generate --check in CI to catch stale ones. The README walks through the setup in Configure and generate. The join tables and foreign keys come from momo migrate diff and momo migrate apply, see Create and apply the migration.

Tag options for relations:

  • fk:<Field> is required for belongs_to, has_one and has_many. For belongs_to it names the foreign-key field on the parent (the model that declares the relation). For has_one and has_many it names the field on the child.
  • join:<table> is required for many2many. The join columns are named after each model and its primary key column, for example document_id and tag_id. Rules:
  • Set join: (same table) on every many2many side you declare. The reverse side is optional, but a reverse side declared without join: makes the generator report a diagnostic.
  • A many-to-many to the model's own type is not supported.
  • Both models need a primary key.
  • The join table has exactly two key columns, named <model>_<pkcol>. Extra join-table columns are not modelled by this guide; use an explicit join model such as a Tagging struct for those.
  • polytype:<column> together with polyvalue:<value> makes a has_one or has_many polymorphic: the child row belongs to the parent only when its type column equals the value.
  • fk_name:<name> names the foreign key constraint of a belongs_to instead of the derived <table>_<column>_fkey (for example _fkey1 on a partitioned table). MomoConfig can do the same with c.FKName(&m.AuthorID, "name"); the field is the key field. Declaring it both ways is an error. A migration diff and baseline compare the constraint by this name. Changing it later is a drop and add of the foreign key (a rename is not generated). A name longer than 63 bytes, a repeated name on one table, fk_name on has_one/has_many and a FKName whose field is not the key of a belongs_to are generator errors. generate --from-db writes it only for names made of letters, digits, _ and $; any other foreign key name is reported and left out.
  • on_delete, on_update and no_constraint affect only the foreign key emitted for belongs_to. has_one and has_many create no constraint, and many-to-many join tables always get two foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE.

momo generate reads these tags and writes one descriptor per relation field into the model's package. The descriptor holds the relation name and kind, the parent and child tables, the key columns, Through for the join table of a many-to-many relation, Discriminator for a polymorphic one, and the typed functions that read and write keys and the field itself. You refer to a relation as <model package>.<Field>:

document.Author   // belongs-to: momo.Relation[models.Document, models.Author]
document.Comments // has-many
document.Tags     // many-to-many

The generator reports a diagnostic, and writes nothing for that package, when:

  • a relation has more than one kind, or the field type does not match the kind;
  • the target is not a Momo model;
  • fk is missing, or names a field that does not exist;
  • many2many has no join:, or a declared reverse side has no join:;
  • polytype is given without polyvalue or the other way round, or polytype is used on a relation that is not has_one or has_many;
  • the polytype column is not a field of the target.

A belongs_to is keyed by its own fk field against the target's primary key, so the referencing model may have any primary key, including a composite one that contains the foreign key column. For example exams with primary key (license_id, exam_id) can declare License *License with momo:"belongs_to,fk:LicenseID", which emits a foreign key from license_id to the licenses table's license_id column and matches a live database that already has that constraint. The target of a belongs_to must have a single-column primary key: a foreign key to a composite target key is refused with a diagnostic that names the target's key columns. A has_one or has_many needs a single-column primary key on the parent, and the child may have a composite key. many2many needs a single-column primary key on both models. Other composite-key relations work with hand-written descriptors but cannot be expressed with tags.

Generated relation field values (Document.Comments) are only ever written by Momo when you load them or list them for CreateGraph. A plain Insert or Update never touches a relation field.

docs.title: 2. Eager loading
docs.text:
momo.Load loads one relation for a slice of parents and assigns the result onto each element. momo.LoadAll loads several.

docs, err := momo.Select[models.Document](db).Limit(20).All(ctx)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := momo.Load(ctx, db, docs, document.Comments); err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := momo.LoadAll(ctx, db, docs, document.Author, document.Tags); err != nil {
    return err
}

The cost is one statement per relation (per bind-limit chunk, see Chunking), not one per parent. Parent order and length never change. Parents with a NULL key get an empty association: a nil pointer or a nil slice.

Behavior to rely on:

  • Associations are cleared before anything is assigned. A parent that matches no children ends up empty rather than stale, and a load that fails part-way leaves empty associations, never partial ones.
  • Soft-deleted children are excluded by default when the child model has a soft-delete column, as in Select.
  • A to-one child shared by several parents is copied shallowly for each parent. Pointers inside the child, including relations loaded with Then, are shared among those copies.
  • A has-one relation that matches more than one child for a parent fails with ErrTooManyRows.
  • With no parents, LoadAll returns nil and runs nothing.

docs.title: Scoping a load
docs.text:
Relation.Scope takes load options for the child statement:

Option Effect LoadWhere[C] extra predicates on the child table LoadOrderBy[C] child order; the relation key and child primary key are always appended as tie-breakers, so order is stable LoadPerParentLimit[C] keep at most n children per parent (top-N) LoadWithDeleted[C] include soft-deleted children LoadOnlyDeleted[C] only soft-deleted children

Load accepts the same options directly after the relation. Use Scope when you pass the relation to LoadAll or Preload:

err := momo.Load(ctx, db, docs, document.Comments,
    momo.LoadWhere[models.Comment](comment.Approved.Eq(true)),
    momo.LoadOrderBy[models.Comment](comment.ID.Desc()),
    momo.LoadPerParentLimit[models.Comment](3),
)

err = momo.LoadAll(ctx, db, docs,
    document.Author,
    document.Comments.Scope(momo.LoadPerParentLimit[models.Comment](3)),
)

LoadWhere filters before the per-parent limit is applied, so "the three newest approved comments" is what the example above loads.

LoadPerParentLimit uses a window function, so the load stays one statement per chunk. It needs PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, MariaDB 10.2 or SQLite 3.25 or later. It applies to has-many and many-to-many relations only. On belongs-to and has-one it fails with ErrUnsupported, and a negative n fails with ErrValidation, both before any statement runs. Zero means unlimited. For a many-to-many relation whose child has a primary key, duplicated join-table rows share a rank and cannot use up the limit. Without a child primary key, each duplicated row takes a rank and can count against the limit.

LoadWithDeleted and LoadOnlyDeleted replace each other: the last one given wins. They have no effect on a child model without a soft-delete column.

docs.title: Nested loads
docs.text:
Relation.Then loads relations on the children, in one pass over all children of the level above:

err := momo.LoadAll(ctx, db, authors,
    author.Documents.Then(document.Comments),
)

Nested loads run over the children that were kept, so combined with a per-parent limit they only load for the survivors.

Scope and Then combine on one relation. Both return a RelationLoader, which has Scope and Then methods itself, so a filtered, ordered relation with nested loads is one loader ("approved comments, newest first, each with its author"):

err := momo.LoadAll(ctx, db, documents,
    document.Comments.Scope(
        momo.LoadWhere[models.Comment](comment.Approved.Eq(true)),
        momo.LoadOrderBy[models.Comment](comment.ID.Desc()),
    ).Then(comment.Author),
)
  • API note: Relation.Scope and Relation.Then used to return Loader[P] and now return RelationLoader[P, C], which implements Loader[P]. Passing them to Load, LoadAll, Preload or Then, or assigning them to a Loader[P], compiles unchanged. Only code that declares a variable with the inferred type and then assigns a different loader to it needs a var l momo.Loader[P] declaration.
  • Scope(...).Then(...) and Then(...).Scope(...) are the same loader. Calling either more than once accumulates: predicates AND together, order items append, a later LoadPerParentLimit replaces an earlier one, nested loaders append. A RelationLoader is a value, so a base loader can be shared.
  • The options apply to this relation's children only. Nested loaders carry their own options, so author.Documents.Then(document.Comments.Scope(...)) scopes the comments, not the documents.
  • The nested level runs once over exactly the children that survived the options, so the statement count stays one per bind-limit chunk at the top and one per level below it. A child excluded by LoadWhere is never a nested parent.
  • With no options and no nested loaders a RelationLoader behaves like the plain relation. An error or cancelled context at the nested level is returned from LoadAll.

docs.title: Chunking
docs.text:
Parent keys are sent as bind parameters, and every dialect caps how many a statement may carry. Momo splits the parent keys into chunks that fit under the dialect's limit and runs one statement per chunk, so a load of any size works. WithMaxParams(n) lowers the limit for a DB. Use it for tests that want to exercise chunking with small data, or for databases configured below the dialect's default:

db := momo.New(drv, momo.WithMaxParams(100))

If a scope alone binds so many arguments that no key fits under the limit, the load fails with ErrValidation before any statement runs.

docs.title: Counting children for many parents
docs.text:
Relation.Count counts one parent per statement. To show a count next to each row of a list, LoadCounts counts all parents at once: one grouped SELECT key, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY key per bind-limit chunk.

counts, err := momo.LoadCounts(ctx, db, docs, document.Comments,
    momo.LoadWhere[models.Comment](comment.Approved.Eq(true)))
// counts[i] is the number of approved comments of docs[i]
  • The result has one entry per parent, in parent order. A parent with no children or a NULL key counts zero; parents sharing a key share the count.
  • Has-one, has-many (including polymorphic) and many-to-many relations are supported, with composite keys. Belongs-to fails with ErrUnsupported, as Count does.
  • The load options that narrow the children apply: LoadWhere, and the soft-delete default with LoadWithDeleted and LoadOnlyDeleted. LoadOrderBy is ignored; LoadPerParentLimit fails with ErrValidation.
  • Many-to-many counts join-table rows, like Count. The far table is joined when it has a soft-delete column and LoadWithDeleted is not set, or when a LoadWhere filter applies. Otherwise nothing is joined, so join rows whose far row no longer exists (dangling rows) are counted too.
  • Parent keys are chunked under the dialect bind limit (see Chunking), and a relation hook sees one event per call.

To order or filter parents by their child count inside a query, use CountOrder (section 5).

docs.title: 3. Preload and single-query loading
docs.text:
SelectQuery.Preload attaches loaders to a query. All, One and First run them after the rows are read, with the same statements LoadAll would use. Preload returns a copy, so a base query can be reused, and a query with no result rows runs no relation statement. Inside a transaction the loads run in that transaction.

docs, err := momo.Select[models.Document](db).
    Preload(document.Author, document.Comments.Scope(
        momo.LoadPerParentLimit[models.Comment](3))).
    Limit(20).
    All(ctx)

Each and Iter stream rows without collecting them, so they cannot batch relation loads. With preloads they return ErrUnsupported.

docs.title: Joined
docs.text:
Relation.Joined() folds a belongs-to relation into the parent statement as a LEFT JOIN, so it costs no extra round trip. Pass it to Preload. It does not work with Load, LoadAll, Scope or Then. A matched joined child with NULL in a column its Go field cannot hold fails with ErrValidation and an error naming the child column (column=...).

docs, err := momo.Select[models.Document](db).
    Preload(document.Author.Joined(), document.Comments).
    Limit(20).
    All(ctx)

Here Author arrives with the document rows, and Comments is still loaded with a second statement. Restrictions:

  • To-one belongs-to only, and only when the relation's child key is the child's primary key or a single unique column. That is what guarantees the join cannot multiply parent rows, so Limit, Offset, OrderBy and Where of the parent query keep their meaning. Has-one, has-many and many-to-many fail with ErrUnsupported when the query runs.
  • Not with GroupBy, Having or row locking on the same query (FOR UPDATE cannot lock the nullable side of an outer join), and not with Each or Iter. All of these return ErrUnsupported.
  • If the query sets its own select list with Columns, it must have one expression per mapped field, or the query fails with ErrValidation.
  • The parent's columns are qualified by the parent table in the select list, so a raw, unqualified column name in the parent's Where can become ambiguous with the joined table's columns. Qualify raw column names.
  • Semantics match Load for belongs-to: a NULL foreign key, or a key that matches no child, leaves the field nil (never a zero struct), soft-deleted children are excluded by a condition in the ON clause so the parent row survives, and each parent gets its own copy of a shared child.
  • A joined load runs no statement of its own, so it emits no RelationEvent. The parent statement is reported to the query hook as usual.

docs.title: 4. Pipelined loading
docs.text:
LoadAll (and so Load and Preload) works in levels: the top level holds the relations you listed, and each Then adds a level. On a connection whose driver implements Batcher, which the pgx driver does on the pool, on a transaction and on a pinned connection, all statements of a level, including every bind-limit chunk, are sent in one round trip. Other drivers (the database/sql adapters, SQLite, MySQL) load sequentially. The result is the same either way. There is nothing to enable and no per-call opt-out.

Two differences to know about:

  • Memory. A pipelined level buffers all of its child rows before assigning any, so peak memory is roughly twice that of sequential loading, which holds one relation's rows at a time. Large child sets with a per-parent limit or a LoadWhere stay cheap; an unscoped load of a huge has-many does not.
  • Hook event order. Sequential loading interleaves each relation's events with its statements. A pipelined level reports BeforeRelation for every relation, then BeforeQuery for every statement and one round trip, then AfterQuery per statement as result sets are read, then nested loads, assignment and AfterRelation per relation. The batch runs under the context of the first statement's hooks, so cancelling that context stops the whole batch, and a statement's AfterQuery duration includes its wait for the batch.

A batch is all or nothing: if one statement fails, every relation's AfterRelation reports the error and the parents keep the empty associations. If the driver rejects the batch before sending anything (ErrUnsupported with Op "batch"), Momo falls back to sequential loading for that level.

docs.title: 5. Relation predicates and traversal
docs.text:
Relations also filter and order queries without loading anything.

// Documents with at least one approved comment.
withApproved := momo.Select[models.Document](db).
    Where(document.Comments.Has(comment.Approved.As("momo_r").Eq(true)))

// Documents without any comments.
quiet := momo.Select[models.Document](db).Where(document.Comments.HasNo())

// Documents ordered by number of comments, most-commented first.
busy := momo.Select[models.Document](db).
    OrderBy(document.Comments.CountOrder(momo.DirDesc), document.ID.Asc())
  • Has(scope...) renders EXISTS (...) over the child table, correlated with the parent through the relation's key columns. It is always a subquery, never a join, so it cannot duplicate parent rows.
  • HasNo(scope...) renders NOT EXISTS.
  • HasFrom(parentAlias, scope...) is Has with an explicit parent alias. Self-referencing relations need it: when the outer query aliases the parent table, pass that alias so the subquery correlates with the right instance.
  • CountOrder(dir) orders parents by their number of children, using a correlated COUNT(*). dir is momo.DirAsc or momo.DirDesc.
  • Soft-deleted children do not count. For many-to-many relations the join table gets no soft-delete filter: only the child table's marker applies.

Scope predicates must name the child through the alias momo_r, because the subquery owns that alias. Build them with As on the generated column: comment.Approved.As("momo_r").Eq(true). A predicate that uses the column without the alias refers to the outer query's table.

Relation.From(parents) goes the other way: it returns a SelectQuery[C] of the children whose key is in the key set of the given parent query. The parent query is embedded as a subquery, so no parent row is fetched:

comments := document.Comments.From(
    momo.Select[models.Document](db).Where(document.ID.Eq(int64(1))))
rows, err := comments.All(ctx)

From does not support many-to-many relations. The returned query fails with ErrValidation when it runs.

docs.title: 6. Association helpers
docs.text:
Link, Unlink, Replace and Count write and count the link itself, with no model in between:

doc := models.Document{ID: 1}
tags := []*models.Tag{{ID: 1}, {ID: 2}}

err := document.Tags.Link(ctx, db, &doc, tags...)    // add pairs
err = document.Tags.Unlink(ctx, db, &doc, tags[0])   // remove one pair
err = document.Tags.Replace(ctx, db, &doc, tags[1])  // make this the whole set
n, err := document.Tags.Count(ctx, db, &doc)         // how many are linked

They only need the keys of the parent and children. They never modify the values you pass in.

They write SQL directly. Model hooks, field hooks and an UpdatedAt column are not touched. Use the model's own update path when those must run.

Statement contract, per relation kind (one statement per chunk; a small call is one statement):

Call Has-one, has-many Many-to-many Link UPDATE child SET fk = ? WHERE pk IN (...); a polymorphic relation also sets the discriminator INSERT into the join table that skips existing pairs (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; MySQL ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE with a no-op); relies on a primary or unique key over the join columns Unlink UPDATE child SET fk = NULL WHERE fk = ? AND pk IN (...); a polymorphic relation also adds the discriminator predicate DELETE FROM join WHERE parent cols = ? AND (child cols) IN (...) Replace diff, then unlink the removed and link the added same Count SELECT COUNT(*) over the children counts join rows, joined to the far table when it has a soft-delete column

What this means in practice:

  • Join tables need a unique key. Many-to-many Link relies on a primary or unique key over the join columns to detect an existing pair. Join tables generated from many2many tags already have a composite primary key over the two columns, plus two foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE. A hand-written join table needs a primary or unique key too, or Link inserts duplicate rows.
  • Has-one and has-many Unlink and Replace need a nullable foreign key, because they clear it. On a NOT NULL column they fail with ErrNotNullViolation, with a message saying so. Delete the children instead if they cannot exist without a parent. For the same reason they cannot be used when the child's foreign key column is part of its primary key (for example exams keyed by license_id, exam_id): the database rejects the NULL. Delete those children instead.
  • Replace is a transaction. On a *DB it opens one, on a *Tx it runs in a savepoint. With no children it clears the set in one statement. Otherwise it reads the current child keys, diffs them in Go against the requested set, unlinks only the removed keys and links only the added ones, in chunks, so kept children are not rewritten and a set of any size works.
  • Replace locks the parent row (SELECT 1 ... FOR UPDATE) on PostgreSQL and MySQL, so concurrent Replace calls on the same parent run one after the other. SQLite serialises writers and skips the lock. Replace needs a transaction, so on a *DB pinned with OnConn it fails with ErrUnsupported (Op "begin"); run it on the pool or inside a *Tx. Link, Unlink and Count accept a pinned handle. The lock is a row lock: a parent that does not exist locks nothing. On a *Tx the lock is held until the caller's transaction ends. Link and Unlink take no parent lock and can interleave with a concurrent Replace.
  • Belongs-to is not linkable. Every helper returns ErrUnsupported. Set the foreign key on the parent and update it.
  • Link, Unlink and Replace return ErrValidation when the parent key is NULL, or when a child key (the child primary key, or the join key for many-to-many) is NULL. Link and Unlink with no children are no-ops that issue no statement. Count of a parent with a NULL key is zero.
  • Chunks and transactions. When Link or Unlink needs more than one chunk and the Querier is a *DB, the chunks run in one transaction, so the call is atomic. On a *Tx they run in your transaction without a savepoint. If a later chunk fails, the earlier chunks stay applied until you roll back. Chunk size follows the dialect bind limit, see WithMaxParams.

docs.title: 7. Graph writes
docs.text: Graph writes are explicit. Nothing saves a relation you did not name.

docs.title: CreateGraph
docs.text:
CreateGraph inserts a parent and the children of the relations you list, in one transaction. List relations with Relation.Include():

doc := models.Document{
    Title:    "Hello",
    Author:   &models.Author{Name: "Ada"},
    Comments: []models.Comment{{Body: "first"}, {Body: "second"}},
}
err := momo.CreateGraph(ctx, db, &doc,
    document.Author.Include(),
    document.Comments.Include(),
)
  • Listed belongs-to children are inserted first and their key is copied into the parent. Listed has-one and has-many children are inserted after the parent, with the parent's key (read back with RETURNING when it is generated) copied into each child, and the discriminator set for a polymorphic relation. Many-to-many children are inserted and then linked through the join table. Relations are processed in the order listed.
  • The graph is one level deep. Children's own relations are not followed, so a self-referencing relation or an in-memory cycle cannot recurse. A model that appears as its own child fails with ErrValidation.
  • Every row goes through the ordinary insert path, so field hooks, automatic timestamps, Go-side defaults and validation run as for a plain Insert.
  • Many-to-many children are always inserted, not looked up. A child that is already stored is inserted again and fails with ErrUniqueViolation, which undoes the whole graph. Link existing rows with Link instead.
  • Has-many and many-to-many children are inserted with the chunked bulk insert: one multi-row statement per bind-limit chunk, so 1000 children cost one statement, not 1000. A has-one or belongs-to child is a single insert.
  • The bulk insert's RETURNING rows are matched to the children in insertion order. If the database returns fewer or more rows than were inserted (a BEFORE INSERT trigger that skips a row, say), the graph fails with ErrValidation and is undone instead of leaving children without keys.
  • A dialect without RETURNING (MySQL) returns ErrUnsupported before a transaction is opened.
  • On a *DB the graph runs in a new transaction. On a *Tx it runs in a savepoint, so a failure undoes the whole graph and leaves your transaction usable. A dialect without savepoints returns ErrUnsupported there. A *DB pinned with OnConn also returns ErrUnsupported (Op "begin"), because the graph needs a transaction; run it on the pool or inside a *Tx.

docs.title: FindOrCreate
docs.text:
a := models.Author{Name: "Ada"}
created, err := momo.FindOrCreate(ctx, db, []momo.ColumnRef{author.Name}, &a)

FindOrCreate inserts the model unless a row with the same key columns exists. Afterwards the model holds the stored row, and created says whether this call inserted it.

  • The key columns need a unique constraint. The statement is INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING, so the constraint decides the winner and concurrent callers never create duplicates; the losers re-select the winner's row. Without a constraint on exactly those columns the database rejects the statement. Dialects without ON CONFLICT or RETURNING return ErrUnsupported before any statement runs.
  • When the row exists, all mapped columns of the model are overwritten by the stored values, and its relation fields are reset.
  • A soft-deleted row is not "found". FindOrCreate never returns or restores a row you deleted, and it does not create a second row with the same key: the unique constraint still holds the soft-deleted row's key, so the insert conflicts and the call fails with ErrUniqueViolation (the deleted row is left untouched, and your model is not overwritten). This holds when the unique constraint covers soft-deleted rows, the case FindOrCreate supports. A partial unique index (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) would let a new row in, but FindOrCreate cannot target it: its ON CONFLICT (key) has no index predicate, so the database rejects the statement. For keys that soft-deleted rows release, use Insert with OnConflict(key).Where(...) and DoNothing, then re-select. To reuse the old row, restore it first; to create a new one, use a different key. A model without a soft-delete column is unaffected. This is the least surprising choice: returning the deleted row would hand back data the application removed, and restoring it would undo a delete silently.
  • Isolation. Under READ COMMITTED the conflicting insert waits for a concurrent transaction and the re-select then sees its row. Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, the re-select can miss a row committed after the snapshot and return ErrNotFound. Retry the transaction in that case.
  • An empty key, a key column the model does not map, or a nil model returns ErrValidation.

docs.title: UpsertByPK
docs.text:
err := momo.UpsertByPK(ctx, db, &a)

UpsertByPK inserts the model, or updates the row with the same primary key: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col. It is the one-call form of Upsert(q).Model(m). Generated columns are read back into the model. The primary key, version, soft-delete and created-at columns are never overwritten. Use the Upsert builder directly when the conflict target is a different unique key, or when you want to choose which columns update.

docs.title: 8. Observability
docs.text:
A hook registered with WithHook that also implements RelationHook receives one event per relation load:

type relLogger struct{ momo.Hook } // embed a Hook for the query events

func (relLogger) BeforeRelation(ctx context.Context, e *momo.RelationEvent) context.Context {
    return ctx
}

func (relLogger) AfterRelation(ctx context.Context, e *momo.RelationEvent) {
    log.Printf("%s.%s %s: %d parents, %d children, %d queries, %s, err=%v",
        e.Parent, e.Name, e.Kind, e.Parents, e.Children, e.Queries, e.Duration, e.Err)
}

db := momo.New(drv, momo.WithHook(relLogger{queryHook}))

RelationEvent fields:

Field Meaning RelationEvent.Parent, RelationEvent.Name parent table and relation name RelationEvent.Kind belongs-to, has-one, has-many or many-to-many Parents number of parents the load ran for Queries child statements compiled for the load; a failed load may have run fewer Children children loaded; set only when the statements succeeded, zero on error Duration filled before AfterRelation Err the load's error

Events fire only for loads that execute statements. They do not fire when there are no parents, when the load fails while being prepared (validation or unsupported options), or for joined loads. BeforeRelation may return a derived context, which later hooks and the load's statements see. For event order under pipelining, see Pipelined loading.

docs.title: 9. Errors and limitations
docs.text:
Errors are *momo.Error values. Test them with errors.Is(err, momo.ErrX). The Op field names the operation.

Operation Error When Load, LoadAll, Preload ErrValidation negative LoadPerParentLimit; invalid descriptor; scope binds too many arguments for the bind limit ErrUnsupported LoadPerParentLimit on belongs-to or has-one; Each or Iter on a query with preloads ErrTooManyRows has-one matched more than one child for a parent Joined ErrUnsupported not belongs-to, child key not unique, GroupBy, Having, locks, Each, Iter; used with Load, LoadAll, Scope or Then ErrValidation select list does not have one expression per mapped field Has, HasNo, CountOrder none of their own an error in the scope predicate surfaces when the query runs From ErrValidation many-to-many relation Link, Unlink, Replace, Count ErrUnsupported belongs-to ErrValidation Link, Unlink, Replace: NULL parent key, or NULL child key. Count with a NULL parent key returns 0, no error ErrNotNullViolation has-one or has-many Unlink or Replace on a NOT NULL foreign key ErrUniqueViolation has-one Link that would break a unique foreign key on the child ErrTxDone the *Tx passed in is already committed or rolled back CreateGraph ErrValidation nil parent, a model listed as its own child, a NULL key that must be copied ErrUnsupported *Tx on a dialect without savepoints; identity read-back on a dialect without RETURNING FindOrCreate ErrValidation nil model, empty key, unmapped key column ErrNotFound re-select misses the winner's row under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE ErrUniqueViolation the key is held by a soft-deleted row ErrUnsupported dialect without ON CONFLICT or RETURNING UpsertByPK ErrValidation nil model

Database errors (unique, foreign key, check, not-null violations, serialization failures) are classified the same way as for any other statement.

Known limitations and follow-ups:

  • A tag-declared belongs_to needs a single-column primary key on its target (the referencing model's key may be composite); has_one and has_many need one on the parent; many2many needs one on both models. Other composite keys work with hand-written descriptors but cannot be expressed with tags.
  • Joined covers belongs-to only. Has-one is not joinable.
  • Pipelining has no public opt-out and doubles peak memory for a level.
  • Link, Unlink and Replace bypass model and field hooks and UpdatedAt.
  • Replace serialises concurrent callers only when the parent row exists, and Link and Unlink are never serialised against it.
  • CreateGraph is one level deep and always inserts; it does not match existing rows.

docs.title: Read replicas
docs.text: WithReplicas registers read-replica drivers on the primary DB. The primary handle never reads from them. DB.Replica with an index returns a handle whose reads may go to that replica; it returns ErrUnsupported when that replica is not configured, and replicas do not chain.

docs.title: What goes to a replica
docs.text:
A statement goes to the replica only when it is clearly a plain read: one statement that starts with SELECT, WITH, VALUES or TABLE, or with EXPLAIN, its options (ANALYZE, VERBOSE, a parenthesised list) and then one of those. It must contain none of these words outside literals, quoted identifiers and comments: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, INTO, COPY, CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, REFRESH, EXECUTE, CALL, DO, LISTEN, NOTIFY, LOCK, DECLARE, GRANT, REVOKE, VACUUM, ANALYZE, CLUSTER, REINDEX, COMMENT, SECURITY, IMPORT; no row lock clause (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR KEY SHARE); none of the side-effect functions nextval, setval, lastval, set_config, pg_notify, txid_current, pg_terminate_backend, pg_cancel_backend, lo_import, lo_export, lo_unlink, dblink_exec, pg_reload_conf, pg_switch_wal, pg_logical_emit_message, or the advisory-lock functions; and no dollar-quoted body. A semicolon followed by more text (a second statement) is refused. Anything else goes to the primary. The list is wide on purpose: a false positive, for example an unquoted column called comment, only costs a read on the primary.

These never go to a replica, whatever the handle:

  • every write (Exec), and every transaction, including reads inside one;
  • INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE with RETURNING;
  • locking reads, such as FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
  • raw SQL that writes, such as a WITH that contains DML, or a SELECT of nextval.

One case cannot be detected: a SELECT that calls a user-defined function which writes looks like a plain read. Run such a call on the primary handle or inside a transaction. The classifier is covered by TestReplicaRoutesWritesAndLocksToPrimary.

A statement that goes to the primary because it is not a plain read counts as a write of the unit of work, so the reads that follow it in the same context see its effects.

docs.title: Combining with other options
docs.text: DB.Replica returns ErrUnsupported on a DB built with WithImplicitTx: that option runs every statement in its own primary transaction, so a replica could never be used. A read on a replica runs outside any transaction, so WithTxSetup does not apply to it. Do not rely on a setting that WithTxSetup installs, such as a row-level-security tenant, for replica reads; use the primary handle for tenant-scoped reads.

docs.title: Reading your own writes
docs.text: Replicas lag. Pass a context from NewUnitOfWork through one request: the first write made through any handle with that context is recorded, and from then on reads of a Replica handle in that context go to the primary. Wrap a context with AllowStaleReads to send reads back to the replica after a write when stale data is acceptable (TestReadReplicaRouting).

docs.title: When the replica is down
docs.text: If the replica fails with a connection-class error when a read starts (connection refused or reset, EOF, a network error, SQLSTATE class 08, 57P01 to 57P03 or 53300), that read runs on the primary (TestReplicaFailureFallsBackToPrimary). Other errors, such as a syntax error, are returned as they are, and so are errors raised after rows have started to arrive: there is no retry in the middle of a result set. A cancelled or expired caller context is never retried.

docs.text:
A database is usable when a driver package for it exists under driver/:

  • PostgreSQL: usable through driver/pgxdriver (vector builders: yes). Migrations: migrate/postgres, run by momo migrate.
  • SQLite: usable through driver/sqlitedriver (needs cgo, not on Windows, vector builders: yes) and driver/sqlitepure (vector builders: no). Migrations: migrate/sqlite, library only (momo migrate does not select it).
  • MySQL and MariaDB: usable through driver/mysqldriver (vector storage and builders depend on the server version). Migrations: migrate/mysql, library only (momo migrate does not select it).

Servers the integration jobs run against: PostgreSQL 16 and 17 with pgvector (see below), and MySQL 8.4, MySQL 9.7 and MariaDB 11.8 for the MySQL driver. Vector support on the MySQL family depends on the server version: MySQL 8.4 has no VECTOR type, MySQL 9.x stores vectors but has no distance function, and MariaDB 11.8 has L2 and cosine distance functions (see MySQL and MariaDB).

docs.title: Testing applications with momotest
docs.text:
github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momotest gives your tests a real PostgreSQL database, isolated per test, with your project's migrations already applied. It replaces the hand-written scratch-database helper that every application would otherwise copy.

Do not mock momo.DB, momo.Tx or momo.Querier. The query builders are the code under test; the constraints and the SQL are what you want to exercise.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Point the tests at a server you may create schemas on:
export MOMO_TEST_POSTGRES_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/scratch

The value must be a postgres:// or postgresql:// URL. Use a database you do not mind filling with temporary schemas; a disposable container is ideal.

  1. Embed the migrations in the package that owns the schema, so the binary and its tests share them:
//go:embed migrations
var files embed.FS

func Migrations() fs.FS { sub, _ := fs.Sub(files, "migrations"); return sub }
  1. Keep tests that use the kit behind the integration build tag (or one of your own), and run them with -tags integration. A plain go test then never touches a database.

When the variable is unset, the test is skipped. Set MOMO_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 in CI and the test fails instead, so a misconfigured job cannot pass by skipping everything. momotest.WithEnv reads a different variable.

docs.title: One database per test: New
docs.text:
func TestSignup(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()
    db := momotest.New(t, momotest.WithMigrations(app.Migrations()))
    // db is a *momo.DB on a schema no other test can see.
}

New creates a schema, applies the migrations to it and returns a *momo.DB. When the test ends the pool is closed and the schema is dropped. Code under test may open and commit its own transactions. Use this mode when it does.

docs.title: A rollback per test: NewTx
docs.text:
func TestOverdraft(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()
    tx := momotest.NewTx(t, momotest.WithMigrations(app.Migrations()))
    // tx is a *momo.Tx; everything written through it is gone after the test.
}

The migrations are applied once to a template schema, named after a hash of the migration files, the extension list and the momo version, and kept on the server between runs. The first momotest.NewTx in a test binary builds it (or finds it ready) under an advisory lock, over a short-lived administrator connection; after that success the binary remembers it, and each later test only opens its own small pool and begins a transaction, which is much cheaper than New. A changed migration gets a new template; old momotest_tpl_* schemas can be dropped at any time between runs.

The Tx is adopted: Commit and Rollback on it return an error matching momo.ErrAdoptedTx, so a test cannot make its writes permanent. tx.Tx opens savepoints, so you can test a failing step and keep going. Two limits follow from using one transaction per test:

  • Code that must commit, or that needs two connections to see each other's work, belongs in a test that uses New.
  • Parallel tests do not see each other's rows, but two that insert the same unique key wait for each other until one finishes. Give parallel tests distinct keys.
  • DDL, TRUNCATE and LOCK TABLE inside a momotest.NewTx test take locks that block every other parallel test using the same template until this one ends. Run such tests with New.
  • Identity and sequence values are consumed by a rolled-back transaction, so never assert a literal generated id; compare with the id that Insert read back.

docs.title: Migrations must stay in their schema
docs.text:
Migrations run in a schema of the test's own, with public after it on the search path. Write them unqualified. momotest refuses early, with the file name, a migration that contains CREATE SCHEMA, or CREATE EXTENSION for an extension not listed in momotest.WithExtensions: an extension exists once per database, so it would land in one test's schema and vanish under the others when that schema is dropped. List extensions in momotest.WithExtensions (names are matched in lower case); they are installed once in public.

The check reads the SQL with comments and string literals removed, so a comment that mentions create schema is fine and CREATE /* x */ EXTENSION foo is still caught. Quoted identifiers are kept. Dollar-quoted bodies are checked as code, because a DO block can run CREATE EXTENSION: the cost is that text inside a dollar-quoted string that looks like that statement is also refused, with a message naming the file. Move such text into a normal string, or list the extension.

momotest.NewTx remembers the result of the check and the template name per migration fs.FS value and extension list. Build the FS once, in a package variable or an embed.FS, so that the files are walked once; an FS rebuilt on every call (such as fs.Sub inside a function) is re-read each time, which still works. Only successes are remembered, so a failed read fails one test and the next one tries again. Changing the files behind a remembered FS while the test binary runs, for example rewriting the directory an os.DirFS points at, is not supported.

docs.title: Leftover schemas
docs.text: Cleanup runs in t.Cleanup, so a killed test run (kill -9, a CI timeout) can leave momotest_<hex> schemas behind. They are harmless but accumulate. Drop them on a disposable server by recreating it, or with DROP SCHEMA momotest_<hex> CASCADE for each name in pg_namespace that matches momotest\_% and is not momotest_tpl_%. Template schemas momotest_tpl_* are meant to stay. momotest has no sweep helper: it never drops a schema it did not create in the current test.

docs.title: Fixtures: Seed
docs.text:
org := &models.Org{Name: "acme"}
momotest.Seed(t, tx,
    momotest.Insert(org),
    momotest.Insert(&models.User{OrgID: org.ID, Email: "ada@acme.test"}),
)

momotest.Seed runs its steps in the order given, so list a table before the tables that reference it. All steps run in one transaction (a savepoint when the querier is a *momo.Tx); if one fails, nothing is kept and the test fails. Insert reads generated columns, such as identity keys, back into the rows you pass, so later steps can use them. momotest.Graph inserts a root with the related rows it includes, as momo.CreateGraph does. A step is any func(ctx, momo.Querier) error, so custom fixtures fit too.

docs.title: Fixtures from a file: LoadFixtures
docs.text:
momotest.LoadFixtures(t, q, path) inserts the rows of a YAML file into q, a *momo.DB or a *momo.Tx, for data that is easier to read as a file than as Go structs. The file maps a table name to a list of rows, and each row maps a column name to a value:

authors:
  - id: 1
    name: Ada
documents:
  - id: 1
    author_id: 1
    title: First
  - id: 2
    author_id: null
    title: Orphan

Tables are inserted in file order and the rows of a table in list order, so list a table before the tables that reference it. Columns are written sorted by name and a YAML null becomes SQL NULL. Table and column names are quoted with momo.Ident and every value is a bound argument, so a value is never spliced into the SQL. A table name is one identifier, with no schema prefix. A value is a string, integer, float, bool, null, timestamp or !!binary (read as bytes); a nested map or list is refused. momotest.LoadFixtures writes plain INSERT statements and is tested on PostgreSQL and SQLite; it has not been run against MySQL or MariaDB. A file that is not a mapping of tables to lists of rows, a missing file, and a row the database refuses (a foreign key to a row that is not there, say) fail the test with a message that names the file, the table and the row. Each row is its own statement, so rows before a failing one stay unless you pass a transaction.

docs.title: SQLite without a server: sqlitetest
docs.text:
github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momotest/sqlitetest gives a test a SQLite database with sqlite-vec loaded, without a server and without an environment variable: sqlitetest.New(t, opts...) returns a *momo.DB on a new file in the test's own temporary directory. Every call opens a file of its own, so two databases in one test never see each other's tables and parallel tests do not collide. The database is closed and the file removed when the test ends. The options go to momo.New, for example momo.WithHook, and momotest.LoadFixtures fills it like any other database. The database starts empty: create the tables with your own DDL, for example momo.SQLiteVectorType for a vector column (see Vector search); momotest.WithMigrations and momotest.NewTx are PostgreSQL features and do not apply.

SQLite lives in its own package, and not in momotest, because the SQLite driver is compiled from C sources: a test binary that imports only momotest for PostgreSQL does not build them, and a repository test (TestMomotestAvoidsSQLite) keeps it that way. Only a test that imports sqlitetest pays for them. The driver needs cgo and a non-Windows target; on any other build sqlitetest.New skips the test, the way momotest.New skips when the server URL is unset.

docs.title: Asserting the SQL: AssertSQL
docs.text:
momotest.AssertSQL(t, compiled, want) compares the SQL text of a compiled statement with want, ignoring differences in whitespace. Get compiled from the SQL method of any query (Select, Insert, Update, Delete, a raw subquery source); the statement is only compiled, never sent, so the assertion needs no database and the recording hook sees no statement. Because only the text is compared, put the values in the query and the text in want:

c, err := momo.Select[User](db).Where(user.Email.Eq("a@example.test")).SQL()
momotest.AssertSQL(t, c, `SELECT ... FROM "users" WHERE "users"."email" = $1`)

On a mismatch the failure holds both texts and Compiled.String(), which lists the bound arguments by placeholder ($1, $2 bound). It never holds an argument value, so a value bound from a sensitive column cannot reach the test log.

docs.title: Asserting index use: AssertUsesIndex
docs.text:
momotest.AssertUsesIndex(t, q, compiled, "index_name") runs a plain EXPLAIN of the statement through momo.Explain (never EXPLAIN ANALYZE, so the statement is not executed) and fails unless the plan reads that index. It works on PostgreSQL and SQLite and fails the test on any other dialect.

  • PostgreSQL: the index name must be a whole token in an Index Scan, Index Only Scan or Bitmap Index Scan node. A name that only starts with the asserted one (orders_idx2 or orders_idx-old for orders_idx) does not match. A mixed-case name that PostgreSQL prints quoted ("MyIdx") matches when you pass MyIdx.
  • SQLite: a plan line must say USING INDEX name or USING COVERING INDEX name.

A failure prints the plan, and says so when the plan contains a sequential scan. Small tables get sequential scans on PostgreSQL whatever indexes exist: load enough rows and run ANALYZE first, or use tx.SetLocal(ctx, "enable_seqscan", "off"). The database may echo literal values into a plan, so run the assertion on test data that is not sensitive.

docs.title: Listing the SQL: a query registry
docs.text:
An application that leaves a code generator such as sqlc loses its .sql files, which it may lint statically or freeze for compatibility tests against the previous release. Momo lists the SQL without a database: register each named query as a builder, then ask the registry for the compiled text per dialect.

momo.RegisterQuery(name, build) adds a query to the process-wide registry (momo.DefaultQueries); momo.NewQueryRegistry makes an isolated one for a test. build receives a momo.Querier that compiles but never executes (see momo.NewOffline) and returns anything with an SQL() method: a Select, Insert, Update, Delete or Merge query, or momo.RawQuery for a hand-written statement. Registering a name twice panics, naming the query. The values you bind in build are placeholders and never appear in the listing. Registry.Compile(dialect.Postgres) returns every query sorted by name with the dialect's placeholders ($1 on PostgreSQL, ? on MySQL and SQLite).

The SQL of InsertQuery[T].Model depends on the model's values. A field tagged dbdefault that holds its zero value is left out of the column list so the database default applies, and a registered builder has no real call to set it, so a sample Model call lists a different statement than the application executes unless you set the sample as a real call sets it. To register a stable shape, choose one of:

  • InsertQuery[T].Values with Col.Set(v) for each column: the column list is exactly the columns you name, whatever the values.
  • Omit(DBDefaultCol) before Model: the dbdefault columns are always out of the list, whatever m holds. This lists the statement of a call that leaves them to the database, not of one that sets them.
  • A sample model whose dbdefault fields are set to non-zero values, to list the statement of a call that writes them.

Registering the call you actually make, with the fields set the way it sets them, lists the SQL it executes. InsertQuery[T].Models follows the same rule per column: it leaves a dbdefault column out only when every row holds its zero value.

momotest.QueryGolden writes that list to one golden file per dialect and fails when a query's SQL changed, a query was added or one was removed. Run the tests with MOMO_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 to accept an intended change, and review the diff in code review. It needs no database, so it runs in a plain go test.

To freeze a release for an N-1 compatibility test, copy its golden file to testdata/queries/<release>/postgres.sql. The program below is the body of that test: it reads the previous release's file with momotest.LoadQueryGolden and prepares every statement against the current schema, so a dropped column or table fails the test. PREPARE plans a statement without running it, and the transaction rolls back at the end.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "os"

    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momotest"
)

func init() {
    momo.RegisterQuery("open_tasks", func(q momo.Querier) momo.Compilable {
        return momo.RawQuery(q, "SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE owner = $1 AND NOT done", 0)
    })
}

func main() {
    if err := run(context.Background()); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

func run(ctx context.Context) error {
    previous, err := momotest.LoadQueryGolden("testdata/queries/v1.4/postgres.sql")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("MOMO_EXAMPLE_DSN"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer pool.Close()
    db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

    return db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {
        for i, q := range previous {
            stmt := fmt.Sprintf("PREPARE compat_%d AS %s", i, q.SQL)
            if _, err := tx.DriverTx().Exec(ctx, stmt, nil); err != nil {
                return fmt.Errorf("the previous release's query %s fails on the new schema: %w", q.Name, err)
            }
        }
        return nil
    })
}

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Effect momotest.WithMigrations(fs.FS) Apply these migrations. The directory needs no momo.sum. Without it the database is empty. momotest.WithEnv(name) Read the server URL from another variable. momotest.WithExtensions(names) CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS in public first; with vector the pool registers the codec. momotest.WithMomoOptions(opts) Passed to momo.New, for example a hook. momotest.WithMaxConns(n) Pool size per test: 4 for New, 2 for momotest.NewTx by default.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: Every call opens its own connection pool and, in New, its own schema, so t.Parallel and -race are safe. The one shared step, creating extensions and building a template, runs under a PostgreSQL advisory lock (keyed by hashtext of the names momotest:extensions and momotest:template), so tests in one binary and several test binaries running at once (go test ./...) cooperate. New also opens a short administrator connection to create and, at cleanup, drop its schema. A momotest.NewTx test holds one connection for its transaction, plus the pool's spare. Each parallel test holds a few connections; keep the server's max_connections above the number of parallel tests times the pool size, or lower the pool with momotest.WithMaxConns or the parallelism with -parallel.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: examples/testing runs a small bank-account service through both modes, in parallel, with seeded fixtures. Its test is the reference for how to write yours.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: Momo is pre-v1 and makes no compatibility promise between releases; see the stability policy. Read this page and the CHANGELOG.md entry of a release before you upgrade, and expect that later releases can break more.

docs.title: --from-db writes only the functions the modeled tables use
docs.text:
momo generate --from-db used to write every database function into the MomoConfig of the alphabetically first model. It now writes only the functions that a modeled table uses: the ones its triggers call, its column defaults, generated columns, checks, index expressions and predicates and its policies call, and the functions those functions call in turn (their bodies and argument defaults). A call is found by name, and so is a 'name'::regproc or 'name(args)'::regprocedure literal (also pg_catalog-qualified, schema qualified or with quoted names) and a to_regproc('name') call. Each one is written on the model of the table that uses it. A function that no modeled table uses is not written, and it is no longer in the init snapshot, so a database-wide function that nothing modeled needs does not appear in the models, and the model files no longer change when an unrelated function does.

Triggers and policies moved the same way: they are written on the model of their own table instead of the first model. A function that a view calls stays on the first model, with the view, unless a modeled table also uses it: then it goes on that table's model. After you regenerate, a model file that held other tables' functions changes (a .new file next to a hand-edited one, see "Running it again" in migrations). A function that was written and is no longer used is not in the new init snapshot either; add it to migrate.exclude if the database keeps it and you do not want drift to report it as unmanaged.

SQL that is built at run time cannot be followed. A function that another function reaches only through EXECUTE with a name put together from pieces (EXECUTE 'SELECT ' || prefix || '_target()'), or through any other dynamic SQL, is not written, and a fresh database built from the models then lacks it. If your functions do that, use introspect.functions: all, which keeps the old behaviour:

introspect:
  functions: all # every database function on the first model

docs.title: introspect.only limits --from-db to a list of tables
docs.text:
introspect.only is a list of table name globs, the inverse of introspect.skip. When it is set, a table that matches none of the globs gets no model, no place in the init snapshot, and momo migrate leaves the live table alone (drift, baseline and diff treat it as excluded), so you do not need a migrate.exclude entry for every table you have not moved yet:

introspect:
  only: [accounts, projects, project_*]
  skip: [project_notes] # skip applies within only

A glob matches the table name, or schema.name for a table outside the current schema (only: ["app.*"]), the same way migrate.exclude does. A table in the current schema (usually public) has an empty schema in the model, so only its bare name is tried: only: [public.users] matches nothing when public is the current schema; write only: [users]. An empty entry in only is an error. skip applies within only: a table must match only and not match skip. A skipped table still needs its migrate.exclude entry. An empty or absent only changes nothing.

If only is set and no table matches, --from-db fails with an error that says introspect.only matched no table, instead of reporting an empty database. When some tables match, a glob that matched none is named in a warning, so a typo does not hide in the rest of the list.

What only hides, and what it does not:

  • It hides tables and, with them, their triggers and policies. Inspection does not read a table outside only, so a table the schema model cannot represent no longer fails --from-db, baseline or drift. migrate diff ignores such a table in the snapshot as well, so a snapshot that still holds one never plans DROP TABLE for it.
  • A partition child is a table of its own, so only: [orders] leaves out orders_2024. Name the children too: only: [orders, "orders_*"].
  • A model for a table outside only (one you wrote by hand) is never migrated: migrate diff plans neither a CREATE TABLE for it nor a DROP TABLE for a snapshot table that is outside only.
  • Views, functions, enums and extensions of the modules you have not moved are not hidden: drift still lists them as unmanaged, and --from-db still writes the views and enums. Hide them with migrate.exclude (globs over the name), for example exclude: [legacy_*, audit_log_view].
  • A foreign key from a modeled table to a table outside only is left out of the models and the snapshot, with a warning, and the baseline reports it as a difference. Move the target table into only, or accept the report. The column itself is still modeled, without the relation.

Library users: migrate.Config.OnlyTables and migrate.InspectOptions.Only are new fields. OnlyTables is what introspect.only sets: when it is not empty, a table that matches none of its globs is hidden from drift, baseline and diff, with its triggers and policies, and the PostgreSQL inspector does not read it. The MySQL and SQLite inspectors ignore migrate.InspectOptions.Only and read every table, which is filtered afterwards, so a table they cannot represent can still fail inspection. migrate.MatchObject is the glob rule shared by Exclude, OnlyTables and the inspector. An empty or malformed entry is an error that names migrate.Config.OnlyTables.

docs.title: skip globs match schema.name
docs.text: introspect.skip globs now match the same way introspect.only and migrate.exclude do: the bare table name, or schema.name for a table outside the current schema. A schema-qualified skip glob (skip: ["app.legacy_*"]) that did nothing before, because it was compared with the bare table name only, now takes effect and drops those tables from the models and the init snapshot. Check your skip list for such a glob before you regenerate.

docs.title: introspect.dbdefault: all tags every column that has a default
docs.text:
By default --from-db writes dbdefault only on NOT NULL columns whose default is computed (now(), gen_random_uuid()), so regenerating does not change what an existing model writes. A column such as version bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 is generated as `momo:"default:1"`, and InsertQuery.Model writes 0 for a model that left Version unset. introspect.dbdefault: all adds dbdefault to every NOT NULL PostgreSQL column that has a default, constant ones included, so an unset field takes the default and the stored value is read back:

introspect:
  dbdefault: all

A nullable column is never tagged, because a nil pointer would stop meaning NULL. The zero value now means "use the default" on those columns: a bool or number field can no longer write false or 0 through Model (use InsertQuery.Values). Hand-written models can use the dbdefault tag on any NOT NULL column that has a database default: see "Database defaults" in the AI guide.

docs.title: --from-db singularizes -se plurals correctly
docs.text:
momo generate --from-db turns a table name into a model name by trying singular candidates and keeping the first one the naming preset pluralizes back to the table name. The order was wrong for words in -se: releases became Releas. The rule now is: a plural in -sses, -xes, -zzes, -ches, -shes or -uses (but not -ouses or -auses) loses es; any other plural in -es loses only the s; a short list of words that no spelling rule separates (aliases, biases, canvases, gases, atlases, lenses, irises, tomatoes, buffaloes, potatoes, heroes, echoes, vetoes, caches, niches, quizzes, uses) is listed by name.

The generated model name changes, on the next regenerate, for these tables:

  • Tables releases, cases, courses, responses, licenses, bases, houses, purposes, causes, clauses and uses: Releas, Cas, Cours, Respons, Licens, Bas, Hous, Purpos, Caus, Claus and Us become Release, Case, Course, Response, License, Base, House, Purpose, Cause, Clause and Use.
  • Tables sizes, prizes, mazes, caches and niches: Siz, Priz, Maz, Cach and Nich become Size, Prize, Maze, Cache and Niche.
  • Table quizzes: Quizze (gorm, bun) or Quizz (prisma) becomes Quiz under the gorm, bun and prisma presets; momo gives Quizz and ent gives Quizze (see below).
  • Table waltzes: Waltz becomes Waltze, because a -zes word is read as -ze, as in sizes.

Not every preset can give every word the right name. The gorm and bun presets pluralize a word that ends in s to itself, and ent matches its rules case-sensitively on the Go name, so some words keep a wrong name there: ent gives Statuse, Buse, Quizze and Aliase; momo gives Quizz (it pluralizes quiz to quizes); gorm, bun and ent give Biase, Canvase, Gase, Atlase, Lense and Irise; -oes words get Tomatoe style names under presets with no -oes rule (momo, ent, and gorm and bun for potatoes, heroes, echoes and vetoes). These were wrong before too.

To keep an old name, or to fix a wrong one, pin it in momo.yaml; the pin wins over the guess:

introspect:
  tables:
    <table>: { name: Releas }

for example releases: { name: Releas }. A regenerate renames the struct in the generated file, so update the code that uses it, or pin the old name first.

docs.title: github.com/google/uuid types need no type tag
docs.text:
A model or projection field of uuid.UUID, *uuid.UUID or []uuid.UUID from github.com/google/uuid now maps to uuid or uuid[] on PostgreSQL (TEXT on SQLite; []uuid.UUID has no SQLite column) with no momo:"type:uuid" tag. A tag you already wrote is still honored and can stay or go. The generator recognizes the type by its import path, so it adds no dependency to momo. Your own module imports github.com/google/uuid only because your models already do. arrayop predicates on a []uuid.UUID column bind with a ::uuid[] cast, like []types.UUID.

momo generate --from-db keeps writing types.UUID unless you set introspect.uuid: google in momo.yaml; then every uuid column becomes uuid.UUID (*uuid.UUID when nullable) and every uuid[] column []uuid.UUID, with no type tag and an import of github.com/google/uuid. An introspect.types rule for uuid still wins. A --from-db re-run after you set the switch regenerates the model files that nobody edited; edited files conflict as usual.

The mapping is for PostgreSQL and SQLite. On MySQL these types are unsupported, as types.UUID is, and introspect.uuid has no effect there. A named type over uuid.UUID (type ID uuid.UUID) is not mapped; give it type:uuid.

docs.title: Query and QueryRows read into a plain struct
docs.text:
momo.Query[T] and momo.QueryRows[T] now accept any struct, with no generated metadata: fields scan by column name (momo:"column:x" tag, else the snake_case of the field name), and a result column with no field, or a field with no result column, is an ErrValidation that names it. A model, projection or Row1..Row10 still scans through its generated metadata. The type parameters changed from [T any, PT Modeler[T]] to [T any]: a call that names only T compiles as before, and a call that named PT explicitly must drop it. A type that is not a struct and has no metadata is now an ErrValidation at run time instead of a compile error: Query[*Task] (a pointer type) now fails at run time, not at compile time.

A struct without generated metadata, for example a model before go generate has run or after a stale generation, now compiles and takes the reflection path instead of failing to compile, so a stale or missing generation shows up only at run time. Run go generate, and keep a test that calls Query for each model.

docs.title: New: One on writes with RETURNING
docs.text:
InsertQuery.One, UpdateQuery.One and DeleteQuery.One run the statement and return the single returned row as T, so a sqlc :one style write no longer needs the Rows / ScanModel / Close loop. Without a Returning list it returns every column. It returns ErrNotFound when no row came back (an ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING insert, or a guarded update or delete that matched nothing) and ErrTooManyRows when more than one did.

Without WithImplicitTx or an explicit transaction the statement has already changed every matched row; run One inside db.Tx and roll back on ErrTooManyRows. InsertQuery.One is for a single-row insert: a multi-row Models insert is ErrValidation, use Rows. AfterLoad runs before the write commits, so an AfterLoad error rolls the write back, unlike SelectQuery.One. MySQL has no RETURNING and returns ErrUnsupported; momo has no RETURNING form for MariaDB UPDATE and DELETE (MariaDB itself has DELETE ... RETURNING), so those return ErrUnsupported. This is additive; nothing to change.

docs.title: The Using and From guard is stricter
docs.text:
UpdateQuery.From and DeleteQuery.Using refuse a statement whose Where does not reference the target table, with ErrUnfilteredMutation. The guard now follows Or, Not and JoinSQL: an Or counts only when every branch references the target, an And when any term does, and Not swaps the two rules. JoinSQL with AND or OR follows the same rules, and JoinSQL with any other separator never counts. Statements that passed in 0.5.0 and are now refused: Where(momo.Or(PostCols.ID.Eq(1), SrcCols.Title.Eq("x"))), where one Or branch is off the target, and Where(momo.Not(momo.And(PostCols.ID.Eq(1), SrcCols.Title.Eq("x")))), which is an Or of negations.

Add a condition on the target to every branch, or call AllRows() when the statement is meant to touch every row. The guard checks that the condition references the target, not that it restricts it: t.id = t.id still passes.

docs.title: OpenAPI error bodies use the key error
docs.text: The OpenAPI document and the generated handlers now describe and send errors as {"error": "<message>"}. The Error schema property was message in 0.4.0. A client that reads message from an error response must read error. Error messages are fixed strings: a constraint violation no longer shows the table or constraint name.

docs.title: Generated handlers and servers
docs.text:
The ecosystem generators (graphql, grpc, openapi, enabled in the plugins: section of momo.yaml) generate servers that do no authentication and no authorization. Wrap the http.ServeMux, the grpc.Server or the GraphQL handler. Turn off operations of the openapi and grpc servers with ops or read_only: true (the graphql plugin has neither option); see the capabilities page for the options, the error mapping, the update semantics and the GraphQL limits.

PUT and gRPC Update differ on purpose. An OpenAPI PUT must carry every required property and writes only the properties it carries, so a property it leaves out keeps whatever value the database has, including one a concurrent request just wrote. A gRPC Update has no way to leave a scalar out (a proto3 scalar at its zero value is a value), so it writes every writable column the message holds; a vector, a timestamp or a defaulted scalar left unset is not written. Neither reads the row first and writes it back.

docs.title: View models no longer produce a table
docs.text:
A model that embeds momo.View maps a view, so the generated schema, and with it momo migrate diff, holds no table for it. A view model gets no CREATE TABLE, and a foreign key never points at it. Declare the view itself with c.View in MomoConfig.

The generated servers expose only list and get for a view model: there is no create, update or delete route, RPC or mutation, and naming a write operation for a view model in ops is a generator error.

If you add momo.View to a model whose table really exists in the database, momo migrate diff now plans a DROP TABLE for that table (AutoMigrate skips it). Review the diff before you apply it.

momo.RefreshMaterializedView refreshes a materialized view (PostgreSQL only).

docs.title: OpenAPI input and output schemas
docs.text:
The OpenAPI document now has two schemas per model. <Model> (for example Document) is the output: every column, with the not-null columns, the key included, listed in required. A client generator now types id as required on a response. <Model>Input (DocumentInput) is new and is what a create and a PUT take: only the writable properties, so it has no key and no read-only, identity or serial column, and its required list is what it was on <Model> in 0.5.0 (not null, no database default). Every response keeps referencing <Model>; the request bodies of create and PUT now reference <Model>Input. A client generated from the old document sends the same JSON and keeps working; regenerate it to get the new types. A model whose name plus Input is also a model name (Doc and DocInput) is a generator diagnostic.

The gRPC messages are unchanged: a model message is still what a client sends and receives. The field comments in the .proto file say which fields a request ignores (the key on Create, read-only columns on Create and Update, and the version, soft-delete and timestamp columns on Update).

docs.title: Error hook and cancellation codes
docs.text:
The openapi and grpc plugins take the option on_error, the name of a Go function in the generated package with the signature func(ctx context.Context, op string, err error). The generated code calls it once for every error it answers from a statement (a database error, a missing row, a cancelled context), with the operation (the operationId for OpenAPI, for example getDocument; DocumentService.Get for gRPC) and the original error, before it writes the fixed message. Log, count or trace the error there. A panic in the hook is recovered, so it cannot stop the request from being answered. The openapi option needs handlers: true, because only the generated handlers call the hook. Without the option nothing changes.

A request whose context was cancelled is now answered 499 (OpenAPI), Canceled (gRPC) and CANCELED (GraphQL) with a fixed message, and one whose deadline passed 504, DeadlineExceeded and CANCELED. These were 500 and Internal before. A client or proxy that retries on 500 will no longer retry them.

docs.title: Regenerating with --from-db after the dbdefault tag
docs.text: momo generate --from-db now adds the dbdefault tag to every NOT NULL PostgreSQL column whose default is computed (gen_random_uuid(), now(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, nextval(...) and other function calls). A Go zero value is no longer written for such a column: InsertQuery.Model and InsertQuery.Models leave it out, the database default applies, and the value is read back with RETURNING. Review the regenerated models: a bool, number, empty string or zero time in such a field can no longer be written explicitly through Model (use InsertQuery.Values or remove the tag), and a plain MySQL database refuses a zero value with ErrUnsupported because it cannot read the default back. Hand-written models are unaffected until they add the tag. See "Database defaults" in the AI guide.

docs.title: Advisory string helpers take options
docs.text: advisory.XactLockString and advisory.TryXactLockString take a trailing ...advisory.Option (for advisory.Hash64). A call site is unchanged, but the function types changed: code that assigns one of these functions to a variable or field of the old func type no longer compiles. Wrap the call in a closure instead.

docs.title: Model hook methods are now wired by momo generate
docs.text:
momo generate detects methods named BeforeInsert, BeforeUpdate, BeforeDelete and AfterLoad on a model and fills Meta.Hooks with them. Two behaviors change for an existing model after you regenerate:

  • A method with one of these names and the exact signature func(context.Context) error now runs: before inserts, updates and deletes, and after loads. Before, such a method was never called. If you had a method with a hook name that was meant as plain code, rename it before you regenerate.
  • A method with one of these names and any other signature makes momo generate fail with a positioned diagnostic (hook BeforeInsert on Doc must have signature func(context.Context) error), and a hook-named method on a projection is a diagnostic as well (a projection runs no hooks). Fix the signature or rename the method.

If you set Meta.Hooks by hand in a hand-written Meta, nothing changes. Generated files are rewritten by momo generate; the Hooks: field appears only for models that have a hook method.

docs.title: View models
docs.text: A model that embeds momo.View (new) is marked as a view. Its writes fail with ErrValidation. Existing models are unaffected unless you add the marker.

docs.title: Upgrading to 0.4.0
docs.text:
Release 0.4.0 moves feature-specific helpers out of the root package momo into subpackages. Every move is a source break: the old identifier is gone and the new one lives under a new import path. The release notes are the 0.4.0 entry of the changelog.

Why there is no alias: a Go method lives in the package of its receiver type, and the subpackages import momo, so momo cannot import them back to keep the old names. A move therefore deletes the old identifier outright.
